To avoid any implication of USTA affiliation, NTRP labels in the app should carry a disclaimer, reachable by clicking the label, which opens a popup reading:

> **NTRP is a reference framework. This platform is not affiliated with or endorsed by the United States Tennis Association (USTA).**

## The highest-exposure copy is not a band label

Worth fixing first, and independently of everything below. `web/src/components/AboutContent.tsx:75-78` currently reads:

> **Not a homegrown scale** — no need to reinvent the wheel. NTRP is proven, and **the USTA shows how it's calculated**.

That names the USTA approvingly, in our own voice, as the authority behind the scale we use — which is closer to implying endorsement than any `NTRP 4.0` chip is. ## Scope — around 25 surfaces render NTRP as visible text

Grouped by what "clicking the label" can realistically mean, because they are not all the same kind of thing:

- `components/AuthLayout.tsx:46` — pre-login marketing copy

## Scope — decided

**Clickable everywhere, plus the About page. No footer.**

The footer line is **rejected**, and for a better reason than the one it was proposed for: a standing USTA
disclaimer on every screen makes NTRP *more* prominent, which undercuts the very position it is meant to
protect — that NTRP is merely a reference framework we borrow, not a relationship that defines the
platform. A disclaimer reachable from the label says "here is what this label means"; a permanent footer
says "our relationship with the USTA is a standing fact about this product". The latter is the opposite of
the message.

So: **every visible NTRP label is a popup trigger**, and the About page carries the disclaimer inline.

> 추가하려는 기능 또는 개선하려는 부분을 간결하게 설명해주세요.

보상(포인트) 도메인. 보유 포인트 조회, 보상 활동 내역(커서 페이지네이션) 조회 API를 구현한다.
배지·스탬프·쿠폰 조회는 이번 범위에서 제외한다 (배지/스탬프는 별도 이슈, 쿠폰은 제휴 체결 대기).

## #️⃣ 이 기능이 필요한 이유는 무엇인가요?

> 이 기능이 필요한 이유 또는 기대 효과를 설명해주세요.

퀘스티 꾸미기(#14) 완료 후 다음 작업 순서. TourAPI 수집이 보류 중인 상태에서 외부 데이터 의존 없이
진행 가능한 도메인이라 이 시점에 진행한다. 포인트 원장(`point_transactions`가 원본, `user_points`는
집계 캐시)은 이미 스키마·설계가 확정되어 있음.

- `UserPoint`, `PointTransaction`, `RewardActivity` 엔티티/리포지토리 추가 (조회 전용, 세 테이블 모두
  `updated_at` 컬럼이 없거나 일부만 있어 `BaseEntity` 미상속)
- `GET /api/users/me/points`: `user_points` 로우가 없으면 0으로 응답 (조회 시 DB 쓰기 없음)

# ArXiv AI Research Digest — 2026-09-03

## Today's Highlights

Today's submissions reveal a strong convergence on **making LLM-based agents reliable, efficient, and auditable** for production deployment. Multiple papers tackle the *evaluation bottleneck* for agents (EarlyEval, Cliff), while others address *safety and alignment* at the harness-policy interface (SafeEvolve, Bilevel Coordinated Reflection). On the model side, breakthroughs in **4-bit pretraining stability (UE5M3)**, **attention control (Trace as State, Language Models Control Own Attention)**, and **LoRA optimization geometry (LoRA-TSD)** point to a maturing efficiency stack. Notably, **competitive programming reaches gold-medal level** via specialized post-training, and **speech BCIs gain a common benchmark**, signaling readiness for clinical translation.

---

## Key Papers

### 🧠 Large Language Models (architecture, training, alignment, evaluation)

| Paper | Authors | Summary |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| [A Common Measure of Communication for Speech Brain-Computer Interfaces](http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02887v1) | Dulhan Jayalath et al. | Proposes a standardized metric for speech BCI communication rates, enabling cross-lab comparison and clinical progress tracking. Critical for translating neural speech prosthetics from lab to bedside. |
| [User Feedback Provides a Unique Signal that LLMs Can not Detect](http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02859v1) | Shachar Don-Yehiya et al. | Demonstrates that naturally occurring user feedback contains information orthogonal to model predictions, enabling improved alignment without explicit annotation. Challenges the view that implicit feedback is too noisy to use. |
| [The Implications of Linguistic Illegibility for LLM Security](http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02852v1) | James Mickens | Argues that LLM outputs and extracted features can be unreliable proxies for internal computation, introducing "linguistic illegibility" as a new attack surface. Reframes interpretability and safety around mechanistic vs. linguistic views. |
| [UE5M3 FP4 Block Scaling for Stable Language Model Pretraining](http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02846v1) | Robert Hu et al. | Introduces a block-scaled FP4 format (UE5M3) that achieves stable pretraining without randomized Hadamard transforms or BF16 fallbacks, reducing overhead vs. NVIDIA's Transformer Engine recipe. |
| [Language Models Can Control Their Own Attention](http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02737v1) | Namgyu Ho et al. | Shows LLMs can learn to predict which context tokens are relevant, enabling sparse attention over million-token contexts with minimal quality loss. Shifts attention from fixed patterns to model-driven routing. |
| [LoRA-TSD: Tangent-Space Spectral Descent for LoRA via Muon-Style Updates](http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02734v1) | Dmitrii Andriianov et al. | Derives an optimizer that respects the Riemannian geometry of low-rank updates, yielding faster convergence and better generalization than standard LoRA fine-tuning. |
| [Trace as State: Reasoning Traces as Conditional States for Long-Context Transformers](http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02702v1) | Xu Zou, Jie Tang | Formalizes reasoning traces as conditional states, proving exponential memory savings for causal state-update tasks when conditions arrive late. NAVAIR/NAWCAD

Advanced Acquisition Documentation Analysis Prize Challenge
The Central Florida Tech Grove, in partnership with NAVAIR/NAWCAD, is launching a prize challenge to identify innovative solutions for advanced acquisition documentation analysis. The challenge seeks intelligent recommender systems that leverage advanced data science, natural language processing, and machine learning to analyze procurement documentation, identify common acquisition requirements, and recommend strategic contract vehicles that improve efficiency and streamline the acquisition process.

Prize Challenge Dates & Details
Official Challenge Launch
July 30th, 2026
Official Prize Challenge Kickoff for all participants 

Submissions Deadline
September 22nd, 2026, 11:59PM EST
Last day to submit your Prize Challenge solution

Final Demo Day
November 9th, 2026
Finalists Demo their solutions live.

Total Cash Prizes
$150,000
1st Place: $100K, 2nd Place: $50K

Prize Challenge Information

***OVERVIEW***

NAVAIR executes tens of thousands of procurement actions annually. While currently leveraging sophisticated tokenization and embedding models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), there is a critical need to evolve beyond simple document retrieval to unlock the analytical power of data cluster analysis by grouping procurement documents based on their content. The purpose of this competition is to build a recommender system that can analyze a varied population of documents such as statements of work, performance work statements, sources sought notices, and open-source information (such as Congressional testimony) and return a candidate list of contract vehicles for consolidation.

Problem Statement

The challenge aims to develop a fully documented, validated algorithmic methodology capable of evaluating, identifying, and recommending common requirements from disparate requirements documentation (SOWs, PWSs, CDRLs) as well as open-source information (Congressional Testimony, news). The algorithm will automatically produce candidate identification and recommendations for strategic vehicles. This includes consolidating similar requirements into larger vehicles or identifying new strategic contracting vehicles based on future capabilities.

Strategic Contract Vehicles are enterprise scale contracts that allows a large amount of requirement owners to procure items/commodities under the same base contract using streamlined procedures. While strategic vehicles can encompass vast requirements, they must maintain the ability to levy consistent and performance scope requirements to vendors. The benefits of this approach include reduced duplication of effort, improved buying power, maximize contract ceilings, and improve speed of acquisition.

Today’s DoD systems contain sparse databases of information with no systematic way to determine common requirements at scale. For example, if VX-XX has a requirement for engineering services on the flight line, the requirement owner has to establish their own contract. This is one of many locations that needs to buy the same service. A better approach would be to identify similar contracting vehicles that can be utilized to fulfill this requirement. In the current ecosystem, the process relies on an individual with knowledge of existing systems, requirements, and contracting vehicles. In order to streamline acquisition processes, there is a need to automatically identify contracts suitable to be used as strategic vehicles.

Benefits:
The primary benefits include increased buying power, reduction of duplication significant process efficiencies, speed of acquisition, and cost savings that directly support DoD acquisition reform efforts.

Critical Technical Criteria:
Deployment Environment: The solution must be designed for deployment within a U.S. Government-owned and operated Cloud environment, accredited for Impact Level 4 (IL4) data.

# **Arweave’s Perpetual Open Web Hackathon**

## **Introduction**

Welcome to the perpetual, open permaweb hackathon!

At Arweave we firmly believe that the future of the [new web should be open source](https://medium.com/@arweave/towards-an-open-source-web-9ffe201fc044) for the benefit of users and developers alike. We want to help make this a reality, so we’re rewarding developers like yourself for building open source dApps on the permaweb!

The Arweave itself is a global, permanent hard drive. The permaweb is a decentralised, immutable web built on top of the Arweave. Permaweb apps are built using normal web technologies — HTML, CSS, and Javascript — but are deployed to Arweave’s on-chain storage system, making them permanent and available in a fast, decentralised manner. You can get started and deploy a permaweb app in 2 minutes or less.

**Time investment:** One afternoon to one weekend.

**Please note that ALL submissions require approval via the [Discord Open Web Hackathon channel](https://discord.gg/ZdGZ8E29Sr).**

## **Reward**

**$250 in ETH + $50 in AR**
A dynamic and interactive web application that is hosted on the permaweb, along with ideas that contribute added functionality to the permaweb eco system. For example: [Arweave API explorer](https://arweave.net/LHff4F45o7ipDqjoePG0PDG5BD2hLD8xf17OBg4FjRE) & [ArweaveID](https://arweave.net/fGUdNmXFmflBMGI2f9vD7KzsrAc1s1USQgQLgAVT0W0). Ideas that resemble or improve on popular web applications such as [AskWeave](https://arweave.net/HhIjOjxgHYXJU5RVjRYfAR017vbZdujbCSlaA8NQ20U) & [Scribe](https://arweave.net/VOKAC_SYiUzbJrEaIY5SEBh1pf0bGQOd8c7G68nzet4#/) are also encouraged, and all applications must include a nice looking UI. Applications whose core features rely on centralised dependencies are not accepted. 

## **Resources**

You can find the docs for getting started deploying your first permaweb app [here](https://docs.arweave.org/developers/tools/textury-arkb).

The docs for the JS library that allows you to read from and write to the permaweb are [here](https://github.com/ArweaveTeam/arweave-js).

ArConnect wallet API docs can be found [here](https://docs.th8ta.org/arconnect/functions). 

Arweave.app wallet source files can be found [here](https://github.com/jfbeats/ArweaveWebWallet).

We’re providing some free tokens so you can get started building and deploying - grab your wallet [here](https://tokens.arweave.org/#/wallet). For guidance on how to use Arweave web wallets, check out [this user guide](https://docs.arweave.org/info/wallets/arweave-wallet).

## **Rules**

**[Check out ArweaveApps](http://arweaveapps.com) to ensure your submission is substantially different from existing applications on the permaweb!**

### **Successful submissions will meet the following criteria:**

- Submissions must be **your own original work**, and must be **unique or substantially different** from other permaweb applications or submissions to this hackathon
- We are happy to accept forks of other applications, but the featureset must be substantially different or significantly expanded in the forked version
Your app **_must_ interact with Arweave** using ArweaveJS
- Your app **must** include either [ArConnect](https://www.arconnect.io/) or [Arweave.app](https://arweave.app/) wallet integration - keyfile drag & drop login ***will not*** be accepted
- Apps must be **open source, with the full source code available on Github or another open code hosting repository**. Feel free to use whatever OSS licence you prefer
- Applications should be **sufficiently complex**, as judged by the core Arweave team. For example, a simple ‘hello world’ app is not complex enough to receive a reward. Broken/non-functional submissions will also be rejected. You should aim for a minimal viable product that an end-user could reasonably start to use
- Your submission must **include a link to a live, functioning, and running instance of the app itself, as well
title: Open web hackathon: Build a simple permaweb app

Turn real Spark-X2.5 runs into reproducible, discussable edge-agent use cases.

For this challenge, obtain XHToken/Spark-X2.5-4B or Spark-X2.5-1.7B from Hugging Face (or a mirror such as ModelScope), conduct a real inference, agentic, coding, long-context, multilingual, quantization, or training experiment, and publish the complete use case in the corresponding model's Hugging Face Discussions. After publishing it, reply to this event's GitHub Issue with the Discussion link to enter.

Measured while implementing claim D of #8531 (PR #9069). Filed unassigned and
observation-class; routing is the triage seat's call. **Not** a defect in any
shipped behaviour — it is an unresolved identification that changes how the
remaining work on #8531 should be done.

## The observation

Two accepted records in this repo describe the same inherited `ADR-0081` label,
and they do not agree on whether it is identifiable.

**ADR-0093** (twice — the *Relates to* line and the D9 recording) says the label
comes from a record it explicitly declines to name:

    the default-org bootstrap (`plugin-auth/src/ensure-default-organization.ts`,
    referenced in code as "ADR-0081 D1" — that decision record predates this
    repo's ADR series)

**ADR-0105**, in its `Builds on` line, cites a **cloud** record by number, on
exactly the subject the label is used for:

    cloud ADR-0016 (open/paid boundary: 强制免费、治理收费),
    cloud ADR-0081 (`@objectstack/organizations`)

So the same document that carried the unqualified `ADR-0081 D2` label at `:334`
and `:348` also carries a **qualified** `cloud ADR-0081` pointer at `:5`, about
the `@objectstack/organizations` package — which is precisely what the D2 label
was used to mean ("multi-org operation is a commercial entitlement").

## Why this is worth recording rather than shrugging at

The two readings lead to **different remediation routes** for #8531's remaining
claims, and the difference is not cosmetic:

- **If the pre-repo record IS `cloud ADR-0081`** — then `ADR-0081 D1` / `D2`
  were never phantom anchors at all. They are **under-qualified cross-repo
  citations**, and the faithful repair is to write `cloud ADR-0081 D1`, matching
  the convention ADR-0105's own `Builds on` line already uses. Cheap, mechanical,
  and it preserves a real pointer instead of erasing one.
- **If it is some other, genuinely unrecoverable record** — then claims B and C
  need new owning decision records minted in this repo, which is the route
  currently assumed and is a maintainer act.

#8531's plan assumes the second reading throughout. Nothing in this repo
establishes it, and one accepted ADR quietly suggests the first.

## What I could and could not check

I could not read `objectstack-ai/cloud` — the session's credential has no access
to it — so I could not confirm whether `cloud ADR-0081` has a `D1`/`D2`, or what
they say. That is exactly why this is filed rather than acted on: asserting the
identification without reading the record would be the same act that produced
the #8531 defect family in the first place.

For the same reason, PR #9069 deliberately **did not** write `cloud ADR-0081` when
de-numbering ADR-0105's two self-citations. It described the referent the way
ADR-0093 already does and identified nothing.

## Suggested resolution

Someone with `cloud` access reads that repo's ADR-0081 and answers one question:
does it hold the default-org bootstrap (D1) and the multi-org commercial line
(D2)? Then either record the identification in ADR-0093's *Relates to* line so it
stops being an open question, or confirm the record is unrecoverable so the
mint-a-new-record route for claims B and C is settled on evidence.

## Dedup

Searched open issues for `cloud ADR-0081`, pre-repo decision record, ADR anchor
identity, and cross-repo ADR qualification. Control: the same searches return
#8531 and #7963, so the query reaches the corpus. #7963 is the same *family*
(an ADR citing a document this repo never contained) but a different document
and a different question. No hit on this one.

Refs: #8531 (claims B and C are the affected work) · PR #9069 · #7963 (related
family, not a duplicate) · ADR-0093, ADR-0105

## 背景
❤️レイの `AIキーパーソン日本株ウォッチ` は毎時実行されている記録がある一方、ChatGPTスレッド上では 2026-08-08 12:34 JST 以降の報告が表示されない事象が発生した。

この状態では、ユーザーから見て以下を区別できない。
- 正常に実行され、差分がなかった
- 実行はされたがチャット配信だけ失敗した
- 監視自体が停止した

重要ニュース監視としては、見かけ上の沈黙が「異常なし」なのか「監視停止」なのか判別できないのは運用上の重大リスク。

## 目的
ChatGPTの表示・通知とは独立した監査経路をGitHub側に持ち、各監視runが正常に完了したことを後から確認できるようにする。

## 方針
ニュース本文の保存ルールとは分離し、**Operational Heartbeat / Run Audit** として扱う。

- ニュース差分なしでも、run成功のメタデータだけは監査ログへ残す
- `追加情報なし` を研究資産として保存するわけではない
- ニュース本文は従来どおり「重要差分あり」のときだけ `06_Research/News/AI_Key_Person/` に保存
- Heartbeatは運用監査用SSoTとして別領域に置く

## 1 runあたりの記録候補
- 実行日時（JST）
- status: OK / ERROR
- news_delta: 0 / n
- GitHub news write: yes / no
- chat delivery: unknown / attempted（取得可能な範囲）
- optional: checked key persons / source count

例:
```json
{
  "run_at": "2026-08-08T23:34:00+09:00",
  "status": "OK",
  "news_delta": 0,
  "news_persisted": false
}
```

## 保存候補
実装時に既存構造へ合わせて決定する。例:
- `Ops/Monitoring/AI_Key_Person_Watch/status.json`（最新成功時刻のみ）
- `Ops/Monitoring/AI_Key_Person_Watch/2026-08.jsonl`（run履歴）

コミット増加が過多になる場合は、GitHub Issueコメントや日次集約なども比較検討する。

## Pages連携
Issue #109 の AI Key Person Watch ページ上に、最低限以下を表示できるようにする。
- 最終監視成功時刻
- 監視状態: Healthy / Stale
- 最終ニュース差分時刻

これにより「ニュースがない」のか「レイが止まっている」のかをPages上で即座に判別できるようにする。

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] ChatGPTの定期報告が表示されなくても、GitHub側で最終成功runを確認できる
- [ ] `追加情報なし` の本文をResearchニュースログへ蓄積しない
- [ ] 監査ログとResearchニュースを明確に分離する
- [ ] 最終成功時刻から一定時間経過した場合、監視停止/遅延を判別できる

- [ ] 既存TEAM_RULESの変更フローに従い、保存方式・Pagesロジック変更はbranch→PRで実装する

## Summary

Extend `apps-ai` with a Obsidian vault platform.

## Intent

The user has knowledge in their head, Claw has some of it in `MEMORY.md`, and n8n workflows carry no durable context across runs. There is no single place where decisions, observations, playbooks, and project context live that the human *and* every LLM helper can read and contribute to — across tech, homelab, travel, finance, and a global todo, not just infrastructure work. This builds that place.

Two constraints shaped every decision below:

- **Humans originate; agents act — on both axes.** Writes and reads are both agent-heavy: a voice note, a dropped document or tasked research arrives as an agent write; "what do these ideas have in common" is an agent read. Direct human writes are extremely rare (and direct human reads, while more common, are still the minority of human-motivated reading). This inverts the usual conflict model: human-vs-agent collisions are rare; agent-vs-agent drift and staleness are the real risks.
- **Durability/independence, not cost, is the binding constraint.** The canonical copy must stay plain markdown that grep/sed/vim can read in 50 years, never hostage to a paid or proprietary service.

## The documentation of record — restructured 2026-08-29

The design attachments and the phase plan this issue previously carried are superseded by the restructured documentation in `ppat/obsidian-tools`:

| Document | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| [USE_CASES.md](https://github.com/ppat/obsidian-tools/blob/main/USE_CASES.md) | The outcomes on four axes, each with a falsifiable acceptance criterion — the stable contract |
| [DESIGN.md](https://github.com/ppat/obsidian-tools/blob/main/DESIGN.md) | The pillars, invariants and the settled Glossary |
| [docs/adr/](https://github.com/ppat/obsidian-tools/blob/main/docs/adr/README.md) | Every reversible decision as a record — context, alternatives, consequences |
| [ROADMAP.md](https://github.com/ppat/obsidian-tools/blob/main/ROADMAP.md) | All the work in one place: the delivery posture, the value path V1–V6, units, dependencies, open decisions. **Supersedes this issue's former phase table for sequencing** |
| [docs/VERIFICATIONS.md](https://github.com/ppat/obsidian-tools/blob/main/docs/VERIFICATIONS.md) | Every control's proving injection, past and pending — the standing rule remains that a control is proven by making it fire, never by observing that nothing bad happened |

The research canon (CANON-1, CANON-2, FINDINGS-v1) is versioned under [`docs/`](https://github.com/ppat/obsidian-tools/blob/main/docs/README.md) with its authority chain; the decision history this issue's "Decisions taken" section previously narrated is captured in the decision records.

## Where things stand (position: 2026-08-29)

**Delivered, deployed and observed:** the substrate (#3441, #3442 — namespace `obsidian-vault`, RWX volume `vault-data`, headless Obsidian + Local REST API, two path-scoped MCP instances behind LiteLLM, default-deny NetworkPolicies, ExternalSecrets; running at `apps-ai-v0.8.0`); the content foundation (`ppat/obsidian-vault#2` — schema, skeleton, settings lock, 16 property types; the write-path gate proven **in both directions** by violation injection, with the refusal arriving as HTTP 200 + `isError: true`, the fact behind #3484); read replication (`ppat/obsidian-tools#3`, #3443 — committer every 15 minutes in-cluster pushing GitHub; `local-replicator` under launchd on the Mac since 2026-08-28, acceptance closed at 5 of 6 with the sixth relocated to `ppat/obsidian-tools#69`, not waived).

**The delivery gap, ruled harmless deliberately:** `obsidian-tools v0.4.0` (2026-08-01) is what runs everywhere; `main` is well ahead (including the `.obsidian/` overlay fix, `ppat/obsidian-tools#71`); release PR `ppat/obsidian-tools#54` (v0.5.0) has been open since 2026-08-08. Closing a ticket records that something was authored — authored, merged, released and deployed-and-observed are four states, never collapsed.

*
title: feat(apps-ai): Obsidian vault platform

**Scope:** full-plan — a new invariant (main checkout never leaves the default branch), a scenario matrix across claim, resume, corrections, ship, and cleanup, a lifecycle with retention and restore, a packaged script, and CLI verbs; it touches four skills and the conventions.

Parent: #104. Depends on #105. Blocks #107, #110, #114.

## Outcome

One feature = one worktree, reliably. The main checkout always stays on the default branch and clean; every branch — feature, trivial chat fix, release, research spike — lives in `.vegastack/.worktrees/<n>-<slug>/` on `<type>/<n>-<slug>`; an epic's children stack on the parent branch inside the parent's worktree, sequential; a worktree is removed only when it is safe (nothing uncommitted, nothing unpushed, merged or explicitly forced) and only at the right time (after merge by dev-ship; parked ones after 14 days by prune, branch pushed first); the same worktree is reused across iterations and restored on demand. The logic lives in a packaged script (`dev-implement/scripts/worktree.mjs`) that the skills call and `vegafactory worktree …` wraps.

## Out of scope

- Parallel children in child worktrees (#115).
- The dispatcher's use of these verbs (#114).
- Claude Code's `--worktree` / `EnterWorktree` integration (deliberately not used: its location `.claude/worktrees/<name>` and branch `worktree-<name>` differ from ours; the factory manages worktrees with plain `git worktree add`, which also works for Codex and Hermes).

## Rules and edge cases

Scenario matrix (each row is a rule the plan implements and tests):
- New issue (no parent): `git fetch origin <default>`; `git worktree add .vegastack/.worktrees/<n>-<slug> -b <type>/<n>-<slug> origin/<default>`; copy the files listed in dev.md `worktree-include:` (e.g. `.env`, `.dev.vars` — gitignored files a fresh checkout lacks; Claude's `.worktreeinclude` applies only to worktrees Claude creates); run dev.md `commands: setup` (e.g. `bun install --frozen-lockfile`); for Codex add `[projects."<abs path>"] trust_level = "trusted"` to `~/.codex/config.toml` (an untrusted path skips `.codex/` hooks, rules, and project config); ledger records the path.
- Epic parent: branch `<type>/<parent-n>-<slug>`, one worktree, created when the first child is claimed; the parent never gets `ready`.
- Sub-issue: `git switch -c <type>/<n>-<slug>` from the parent branch inside the parent worktree; one child at a time; on the child's merge word dev-ship merges the child branch into the parent branch (no PR); when all children are done the parent gets one PR to the default branch.
- Resume: same branch, reuse the worktree; a fresh session reads brief → plan → ledger → `git log` there.
- Corrections / reclaim: reuse; if the directory is missing but the branch exists, restore (`git worktree add <path> <branch>`, then include-copy, setup, trust).
- Ship PR: ship-gate runs inside the worktree (its checkout==branch check holds by construction; add `--worktree <path>` or auto-resolve via `git worktree list --porcelain`). Merge: per `merge:` knob; then remove the worktree, delete the local branch, prune the remote branch; a parent worktree goes only when the parent merges.
- Rebase onto default inside the worktree; re-verify what the rebase touched.
- Direct chat trivial fix: `<type>/<slug>` in a worktree too. Research: `research/<n>-<slug>` worktree only if code is written; removed at hand-back, never merged. Release: `chore/release-<v>` in its own worktree. Cross-agent review: read-only in the same worktree. Abandoned issue: branch and worktree removed only on the operator's word.
- Lifecycle states derived from git + GitHub, never stored: `active` (session holds it: dispatcher lock or `git worktree lock`), `parked` (issue open, no session), `merged` (branch is an ancestor of `origin/<default>`), `abandoned` (issue closed unmerged), `orphan-dir` (directory, branch gone), `branch-only` (branch, no directory).
- Safe-to-remo
title: feat: one feature, one worktree — scenario matrix, lifecycle, and worktree verbs

## Abstract

A part is data, not code. This feature adds a versioned library — keyed by function code (what the part logically does) crossed with family and package (electrical figures and footprint) — so a design element can bind to a library member the way it already binds to nothing today. Everything downstream — a bill of materials, a wiring list, a netlist a fab tool will accept, a fan-out check, a breadboard placement — becomes a query against that library instead of a table hard-coded in an emitter. The library is extensible by a user with a text file and no Java.

This is the physical programme's first real step, not a standalone parts table: `docs/capability-roadmap/sweep-06-physical-boundary.md` records the same gap under change D ("cells as data, not classes … loaded from a library file") for the eventual ASIC/technology-cell layer, and the drawn-element-to-library-member binding this feature builds is the first instance of a mapping the project will need at least twice more (sky130 cells, KiCad symbols under #307). It is named and scoped here as a technology-mapping seam for that reason, not just as a 74-series lookup table.

Three cuts: a narrow proof slice and binding mechanism first (TASK-0085, filed as #400 — restructured, per its own rewrite, into a single vertical slice on the `ElementType`/registry extension point, with the general schema deferred to a later increment), then the transcribed part data (TASK-0055, filed as #450), and the shared realization-layer contract document (TASK-C349-1, filed as #898, assigned onto this feature's corpus per maintainer directive 2026-08-16). All three are open. A fourth roster entry, #917, sits in `requires_tasks` as well; it was re-homed onto this feature by the v7/v4 ownership migration rather than derived as a cut here. See Status & Dependency Graph.

## Intended Audience & Impact

- **A student building a drawn CPU on a breadboard.** The artifact *is* packages, sections, pins and jumpers. Without part data there is nothing to place. After this, a placement plan and a wiring list are queries.
- **Anyone sending a netlist to a board tool.** A netlist component with an empty footprint field is discarded on import, so the footprint column is the gate between "JLS exports a netlist" and "a board tool accepts it". One string per package opens it.
- **A user who needs a part JLS does not ship.** They add a text file. No Java, no recompilation, no fork.
- **An instructor migrating course material** whose source tool ships its own TTL component library. Parity means the imported design's parts resolve to entries here.
- **An instructor distributing a parts file to a class** (maintainer directive 2026-08-16). The same loader that reads the bundled defaults reads the file the instructor hands out; a student points JLS at it with `-parts` and gets the course's exact part set. This distribution model is load-bearing for §1 item 8's resolution mechanism.
- **A reviewer of an absorbed entry.** Every entry names the datasheet or absorbed source it came from, drawn from a closed vocabulary (see Licensing), and carries that source's license notice, so the library survives an audit rather than being an unattributable pile.

No single child asserts this: the schema without data describes nothing, and the data without the schema is a text file no pass can query.

## Status & Dependency Graph

```yaml
tier: feature
evidence_commit: 2d0ca9dcd9db78b36c3caf4c6c57dd8701862cc7
requires_tasks: [400, 450, 898, 917]  # re-homed unowned task(s) per the confirmed orphan disposition
planned_tasks: []
blocked_by: []
blocks: [365, 366]
serves_capstones: [297, 298]
related: [264, 311]
```

All four roster entries are filed and open. **#400 (TASK-0085)** — restructured, per its own rewrite, into a single vertical slice (one part, `74LS08`, one emitter path) seated on the `ElementType`/registry extension point, with the binding in a side-car file; the general versioned schema this issue describes in §1/§
title: FEAT-040: JLS knows what a real part is — pinouts, sections, footprints and loading are queryable data, extensible with a text file and no Java

Filed while implementing #14100 (unassigned: recording only). #14100 is scoped to exactly 4 `it()` and the 2 `beforeAll` hooks in `sql-driver-backend-fault-envelope.test.ts`, and that scoping is respected — nothing here was folded into its PR (#14212), following that card's own "separate card rather than a rider" precedent.

Two findings, one measured and one structural. The measured one comes first because it reframes the other.

## 1. A hook does NOT inherit the 5000ms default — it inherits `hookTimeout`, measured at 10000ms

Both #13902 and #14100 describe the defect class as work "on vitest's inherited 5000ms default". For `it()` sites that is exact. **For hooks it is wrong**, and the difference was measured in `packages/drivers/driver-sql`'s real config (which sets neither `testTimeout` nor `hookTimeout`, so both are vitest's own defaults):

| Leg | Shape | Result |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | `it()`, 6000ms sleep, no budget | exit 1 — `Test timed out in 5000ms` (5.58s) |
| A2 | `it()`, 6000ms sleep, `60_000` | exit 0 (6.54s) |
| B1 | `beforeAll`, 6000ms sleep, no budget | **exit 0 — passed** (6.46s) |
| B3 | `beforeAll`, 11000ms sleep, no budget | exit 1 — `Hook timed out in 10000ms` (10.56s) |
| B4 | `beforeAll`, 11000ms sleep, `60_000` | exit 0 (11.52s) |
| A3 | `it()`, 11000ms sleep, `60_000` | exit 0 (11.50s) — control |

Probes were run through the shared verify lock, exit codes captured by redirect before any pipe, on-disk landing proven by marker counts, and removed by trap with absence re-proven.

Consequences, none of which change #14100's fix:

- An unbudgeted **hook** has twice the headroom of an unbudgeted `it()`. A hook is therefore a *less* urgent instance of this class than an `it()`, not a more urgent one — worth knowing before anyone sizes the remaining work.
- The third argument demonstrably does lift a hook's ceiling (B4), so budgeting hooks is effective, not decorative.
- Any prose in this class that says hooks sit at 5000ms should be corrected when touched. #14212 corrects it at the two sites it edits.

## 2. Seven unbudgeted hooks whose driver argument is unconditionally live

A per-site AST walk over all 159 test files in `packages/drivers/driver-sql/src` (193 driver-constructing sites total), classifying each site by **reading its `new SqlDriver(...)` argument** rather than by filename, finds these hooks with an unconditionally live cell argument and no explicit budget. None is named by #14100:

| Site | Hook | Argument | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sql-driver-datetime-mysql-storage.test.ts` | `beforeEach` (x3, three suites) | `MYSQL_CELL.config()` | drop table, `initObjects(...)` |
| `sql-driver-datetime-postgres-timezone.test.ts` | `beforeAll` | `PG_CELL.config()` | connect, read `current_setting('TimeZone')`, disconnect |
| `sql-driver-datetime-postgres-timezone.test.ts` | `beforeEach` | `PG_CELL.config()` | drop table cascade, `initObjects(...)` |
| `sql-driver-json-binding-without-ddl.test.ts` | `beforeAll` | `PG_CELL.config()` | connect, out-of-band `create table`, register metadata |
| `sql-driver-time-live-dialects.test.ts` | `beforeEach` | `MYSQL_C

design-evidence ladder ([docs/design-evidence-tiers.md](https://github.com/2AMLogic/klayout-tools/blob/main/docs/design-evidence-tiers.md)).

**T1 and "bronze" are the same rung.** `klayout-tools/docs/design-evidence-tiers.md`
(T1 -- sim-validated) and `product/everyblock/tiers.md` (Bronze) define it in
identical words: *"Designed and simulation-validated with open tools."* Two
vocabularies for one ladder has already caused confusion about what this block's
status is. This epic tracks the **engineering evidence**; awarding the catalog
tier is a separate operator decision, per `tiers.md` ("Who can grant it: us,
unilaterally").

## How this status was derived, and what it is not

Derived **2026-08-09** from this repo's `main` tree via the GitHub API, and
re-confirmed against `origin/main` @ `4c8630b` (2026-08-20 -- see the Curator
re-check in "Verified corrections" below). It is an **artifact-presence
survey**, which is necessary but not sufficient for T1: the ladder requires
every report to be *fresh* (provenance matching current sources) and
*passing*. Presence of a report is not a pass, and this pass did not open the
reports.

So a checked box below means "the artifact exists on `main`"; it does **not**
assert the pass condition unless the note says the verdict was read. Items marked
*unverified* are the ones where the artifact exists and someone still has to

## Summary

`codex mcp login <server> --oauth-client-registration dcr` does not follow the absolute `resource_metadata` URL advertised in the MCP server's `401 WWW-Authenticate` challenge. Instead, it probes only `.well-known` metadata paths on the MCP resource origin. When those paths return `404`, Codex falls back to dynamic registration on the MCP origin (`/register`) rather than discovering the distinct authorization server and its advertised `registration_endpoint`.

This breaks deployments where:

- the MCP resource server and OAuth authorization server are different origins;
- the resource server advertises protected-resource metadata through an absolute, centralized URL in `WWW-Authenticate`; and
- the MCP resource origin intentionally does not serve `.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` itself.

Other MCP clients that follow the challenge's `resource_metadata` URL complete the flow.

## Environment

- Codex CLI 0.152.1 (`rust-v0.152.1`)
- macOS arm64
- `codex mcp login oauth-repro --oauth-client-registration dcr`

## Minimal repro

The self-contained executable reproducer is in [the first comment below](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/42427#issuecomment-5519770828). Save it as `codex_mcp_oauth_dcr_repro.py` and run:

```bash
python3 codex_mcp_oauth_dcr_repro.py
```

It starts three loopback-only servers:

1. MCP resource server: `/mcp` returns `401` with an absolute `resource_metadata` URL.
2. Central protected-resource-metadata server: returns an `authorization_servers` value pointing at server 3.
3. OAuth authorization server: advertises `/oauth2/register` as its `registration_endpoint`.

The authorization server's DCR handler deliberately returns:

```json
{"probe":"advertised-registration-endpoint"}
```

so a request reaching it is unambiguous and does not begin a browser OAuth flow.

Actual result from 0.152.1:

```text
Error: Registration failed: Dynamic registration failed: Registration failed:
HTTP 404 Not Found: {"probe":"resource-not-found"}
```

The mock request log contains no request to the centralized PRM server and no request to the authorization server. It shows only requests to the MCP resource origin, followed by:

```text
POST /register
```

## Expected behavior

Codex should follow the absolute `resource_metadata` URL from the `WWW-Authenticate` challenge, fetch its `authorization_servers` metadata, then post the DCR request to the full `registration_endpoint` advertised by that authorization server.

## Why this appears inconsistent with the current code

`codex-rs/rmcp-client/src/oauth_client_registration.rs` constructs an `AuthorizationManager` and calls `resolve_metadata()`. The same release's `oauth_client_registration_tests.rs` includes `verified_issuer_can_delegate_authorization_and_token_to_one_origin`, which verifies a DCR POST is sent to a delegated authorization-server endpoint.

The reproducer suggests the direct `mcp login` discovery path does not preserve or use the initial `WWW-Authenticate` challenge's `resource_metadata` URL when resolving metadata. That occurs before the delegated-registration test coverage.

## Related issues

- #34684: macOS Codex OAuth discovery failure while other MCP clients work on the same machine.
- #20503: DCR interoperability issue involving registration metadata.
title: codex mcp login ignores WWW-Authenticate resource_metadata during DCR discovery

## What happened

The leaderboard is a Daily Challenge board: one run on one shared deal per date.
A player climbing the ladder has nothing on it, and there is no board for score
earned over time. Meanwhile a Daily clear banks its final score into the player's
total score like any ladder win.

## What I expected

Score belongs to the ladder, and the one leaderboard is weekly.

**The Daily Challenge stops paying score.**

- A Daily clear pays trophies and the streak, nothing else. Its score is not
  banked and never counts toward the player's total score.
- The Daily grants no boosters — it grants none today and must keep granting none.
- Trophies, the streak, the once-per-date credit, and the clear-locks-replay rule
  are unchanged.

**One weekly leaderboard, ranking climbers by score earned.**

- Every ladder clear adds its final score to the player's standing for the current
  week.
- The week starts Sunday 00:00 UTC on the server's own clock, so every player is
  ranked over the same seven days. When it rolls over the board is empty and every
  standing is back to zero.
- Only the live week is browsable — no past weeks, and no daily board.
- **The board shows the time left until it resets** — a plain countdown by the
  board's heading ("Resets in 2d 14h", tightening to hours and minutes near the
  boundary), ticking while the panel is open and announced with the board to
  screen readers. Reaching zero with the panel open reloads it into the fresh,
  empty week rather than leaving stale standings on screen.
- The Daily Challenge board goes away entirely, and the Daily contributes nothing
  to the weekly standing.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Note your total score on the profile, then play and clear today's Daily
   Challenge — total score goes up by the Daily's final score.
2. Clear several ladder levels without opening the Daily Challenge.
3. Open the leaderboard: nothing you scored appears, because the board only lists
   Daily Challenge runs.

## Additional context

- Weekly standings accumulate across runs, unlike today's one-row-per-deal-that-
  only-moves-up model.
- The current score bound assumes a single run (a flawless 144-tile game tops out
  at 20970). That bound has to apply to each score being added, not to the standing
  it accumulates into.
- Opt-in, the screened display name, "withdraw removes every entry", and public
  read-without-account all carry over unchanged.
- The countdown is computed from the server boundary, not local midnight, so a
  player in the Americas watches it hit zero on a Saturday afternoon.
- Move history should keep being stored per submission — the score-verification
  follow-up still needs it.
- Total score is a lifetime counter that also syncs, and existing totals already
  include past Daily clears. The plan is to leave banked history alone and stop
  banking from here on; say if past Daily score should be removed retroactively.

## Decided (PM, 2026-09-03)

1. **Week boundary uses the server clock — Sunday 00:00 UTC.** Not the player's
   local week: a client-supplied week key would split the board into overlapping
   buckets across ~27 hours of boundaries and would need the skew/age guards the
   Daily board carries today. The accepted cost is that the reset lands at an odd
   local hour (Saturday 16:00 Pacific).
2. **The score HUD stays during a Daily run** — it drives the Super Combo
   feedback. Nothing is banked from it.

### What would you like to be added?

This FR requests the implementation of a new SubAgent class: A re-usable component that manages LLM driven tool orchestration. 

This is applicable in the following contexts:
* Allowing a Tool to iteratively solve a problem it encounters. For example, the EditTool using the SubAgent to find a better match string in the case of stale data; or a future "update docstrings" tool, which may call multiple existing tools to find files, edit them and test them.
* Agentic Scopes - Allowing a Tool to be run in an isolated mode - If a tool doesn't manage its' own self healing, and instead expects to do that on the main thread, a SubAgent can be created, which clones the MonoAgent history, executes the tool, and only returns the successful response back to the main thread ()

This FR suggests the most direct path towards implementation would be:
* Create a wrapper around GeminiChat which can drive the GeminiChat::sendMessage*(..) functions either in a nonInteractive, or Interactive function
* Allow a list of filtered tools to be passed to the GeminiChat ContentGenerator::generateContentStream(..) function, so that only a subset of tools may be considered during execution
* Allow a custom system prompt to be provided for GeminiChat to use.
* Allow variable output via a set of private tools that the Agent can use to calculate response data to be accessed via the Caller of the SubAgent.





### Why is this needed?

Currently, GC uses a _mono-agent_ architecture; One SWE Agent which is responsible for all work across the application. While this approach is powerful in its' own right, there's some challenges that it presents:

* Higher Memory Rot - Given that all self healing operations occur in a single History object, there's a higher chance of hallucinations over time as the context history becomes more complex and full of conflicting / stale information. Consider the situation where a file-read occurs, then 2-3 edit attempts that fail, followed by a success. There now may be 5 examples of the same block of code in history memory, which can lead to confusion.
* Lack of SmartTools - The GC Codebase currently has a single agent implementation (GeminiClient + GeminiChat), which means that tools themselves cannot currently support agentic loops in their processing (e.g. recovering from a failure, or orchestrating private tools to execute a task). Further, no other part of the application can engage in Agentic patterns, since there's no primitive to leverage to do so.

### Additional context

Areas of open discussion:
* **Tool permissions** - There's some open discussion that needs to be had about how tool-based permissions work inside subagents. (For example, if you've given ToolX permission to write-always, does that permission also follow forward to when that tool is used inside of a subagent?) 
* **System prompt re-use** - The SubAgent can accept a custom system prompt to drive work, but it may be viable to leverage existing portions of the existing MonoAgent prompt. This is a challenge because the current Mono-Agent system prompt is _powerful_ but also _static_: It currently does not provide a mechanism to be re-used by sub agents, or be broken up in the case of available tools changing. In this case, an ideal solution for SubAgents orchestrating the existing tools may require breaking up prompts.ts to provide a sub-agent the ability to grab examples & multi-shot snippets for a specific tool it is using (which is currently hard-coded into the main prompt).

Important Notes:
* This FR _only_ discusses the addition of the SubAgent primitive, and is not intended to be a solution to larger discussions around mass orchestration of Agents, or their coordinated efforts towards task resolution (e.g. "why not use existing agent-orchestration library X?"). Those are significant architecture conversations that need to happen across the team, as orchestration is a higher level discussion to the SubAgent primitive

# Cron incident feed

**Do not close.** This issue is the notification surface for the auto-capture system wired up in `.github/workflows/log-cron-incident.yml`.

## How it works

- When any allowlisted cron workflow finishes with `conclusion: failure`, the listener appends a row to [`docs/cron-rebuild-failures.md`](../blob/main/docs/cron-rebuild-failures.md) with `Status: OPEN` and posts a comment on this issue with the failed run URL + a log-tail excerpt.
- When the next scheduled run of the same workflow succeeds, the listener flips the most-recent `OPEN` row to `RESOLVED (auto)` and posts a `✅` comment here.
- `BLOCKED`, `FLAKE`, and human-set `RESOLVED` rows are never touched by auto-resolve.

## Kill switches

Repo Settings → Variables:

| Variable                                   | Effect                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `CRON_INCIDENT_LOGGER_ENABLED=false`       | Disable everything (no capture, no auto-resolve, no comments). |
| `CRON_INCIDENT_AUTO_RESOLVE_ENABLED=false` | Keep failure capture; disable auto-resolve only.               |
| `CRON_INCIDENT_ISSUE_NUMBER`               | Issue number for this feed (set once during initial setup).    |

## What goes in a comment

Each failure comment shows:

- Workflow name (human-readable + kebab id)
- Run URL
- Status flag
- Link back to the ledger row
- Last 30 lines of the failed step's logs (in a collapsed `<details>` block)

Each auto-resolve comment shows:

- ✅ marker
- Workflow name + date
- The next-success run URL that triggered the flip

## Manual override

If a row gets auto-resolved but is actually still broken: edit the ledger row directly, change Status back to `OPEN` (or `BLOCKED`), and add context to the Root Cause column. The listener will re-flip it on the NEXT successful scheduled run if the underlying issue is fixed.

If a row should be left OPEN forever (waiting on external action): change Status to `BLOCKED` — auto-resolve skips that exact value.

## Summary

The SDPA compute kernels fold `scale` into the softmax exponent, `exp((QK + mask - row_max) * scale)`, so the
mask is scaled together with `QK`. The prefill entry point knows this and pre-multiplies the mask by `1/scale`
(`ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/transformer/sdpa/sdpa.cpp:56-79`, added by #42891 for #42694, with a comment that
spells out the PyTorch semantics). The same omission in `flash_mla_prefill` (same file, same prefill kernel) is
tracked by #43239 and #55333, and #40470 covers the analogous scaling of `attention_sink`; none of them touches the
decode op, which lives in its own directory with its own compute kernel. The decode entry points in `sdpa_decode.cpp`
forward the caller's `attn_mask` untouched, so
`scaled_dot_product_attention_decode` and `paged_scaled_dot_product_attention_decode` compute

```
softmax((QK + M) * scale)      instead of      softmax(QK * scale + M)
```

Hard masks built from `{0, finfo.min}` cannot observe this (`finfo.min * scale` still drives `exp` to zero), but any
finite additive bias
(ALiBi, T5 relative-position bias, a soft mask, a logit bias) is silently shrunk by `scale = 1/sqrt(D)`: by
5.7x at `D = 32`, by 11.3x at `D = 128`. Two ttnn entry points for the same math therefore disagree with each
other, and decode disagrees with PyTorch. (The two MLA wrappers forward the mask the same way, but they
currently require `is_causal=True` and the validator rejects a mask in causal mode, so they cannot reach it.)
The experimental Quasar port (`ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/experimental/quasar/transformer/sdpa_decode/sdpa_decode.cpp`) forwards the mask the same way while its prefill sibling carries the compensation, so the same fix applies there.

## Reference semantics

`torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention` (ATen `sdpa_math`):
`attn_weight = (Q @ K^T) * scale_factor; attn_weight += attn_bias; softmax(attn_weight, -1)`. The bias is
added after scaling, i.e. unscaled. `sdpa.cpp:56-79` states the same and compensates.
The decode op's own tech report (`tech_reports/FlashAttention/FlashDecode.md`, "Non-causal mode") documents the same reference, `softmax(query @ k_cache^T * scale + mask)`, and says users can pass an arbitrary attention mask.

## Current implementation

`ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/transformer/sdpa_decode/sdpa_decode.cpp:79-95` (and the identical pattern in the
paged entry point at `:157-172`):

```cpp
return ttnn::prim::sdpa_decode(
    input_tensor_q, input_tensor_k, input_tensor_v, cur_pos_tensor, std::nullopt,
    attn_mask,            // raw, never pre-divided by 1/scale
    attention_sink, is_causal, false, cur_pos, scale, ...
```

`sdpa_decode/device/kernels/compute/sdpa_flash_decode.cpp:403` adds the mask to the unscaled `QK`
(`add_block_inplace(cb_qk_im, cb_mask_in, ...)`) and `:442` then computes `exp((QK - cur_max) * scale)`.

## Measured (ttsim, Blackhole, tt-metal `9fa00fc`; bfloat16 Q/K/V/mask)

`b = nh = nkv = 1`, `S = 32`, `Q = 0` (so `QK = 0` on every key and the softmax is driven by the mask alone),
`V[key0] = 1`, `V[other keys] = 0`, `attn_mask = finfo.min` everywhere except `M[key0] = 0` and
`M[key1] = bias`. The output is then the softmax weight of key 0, i.e. `sigmoid(-bias)` in PyTorch.

| D | bias on key 1 | `sdpa_decode` | prefill `scaled_dot_product_attention` (same Q/K/V/mask) | PyTorch |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32 | -1.0 | **0.5273** | 0.7188 | 0.7311 |
| 32 | -2.0 | **0.5703** | 0.8789 | 0.8808 |
| 32 | -3.0 | **0.6172** | 0.9453 | 0.9526 |
| 128 | -1.0 | **0.5039** | 0.7188 | 0.7311 |
| 128 | -2.0 | **0.5273** | 0.8789 | 0.8808 |
| 128 | -3.0 | **0.5508** | 0.9453 | 0.9526 |

The decode column tracks the attenuated-bias prediction `sigmoid(-bias * scale)` (`0.588` at `D = 32`, `bias = -2`,
with some further decode-kernel approximation on top); at `D = 128` the bias is shrunk 11.3x and every row
collapses toward 0.5. Prefill returns the PyTorch value because
`sdpa.cpp:76` compensates. With the compensation added to decode, decode and
title: ttnn.transformer.scaled_dot_product_attention_decode scales the user attn_mask by `scale`: a finite additive bias is attenuated by 1/sqrt(D), unlike PyTorch and unlike the prefill op, which compensates for exactly this

## Summary

`ttnn.prod_bw` computes the gradient as

```text
prod(input) * grad / input
```

which is `reciprocal(input)` multiplied by a broadcast `prod(input) * grad`. Where the input
contains an exact zero, `reciprocal(0)` is `+inf` and the surviving product is `0`, so the
gradient at that position is non-finite instead of the finite value autograd defines.

```text
input:    [2, 0, 4]
grad:     1
expected: [0, 8, 0]
current:  [0, non-finite, 0]
```

This is a source-level analysis: I do not have a card, so the host replay below renders the
device `inf * 0` as a non-finite value without asserting which one appears in silicon. The defect
is that the gradient is non-finite where the correct value is finite.

## Root cause

Both branches multiply by `reciprocal(input)`:

- `dim=None`:
  [`unary_backward.cpp#L1668-L1676`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/a5cd86212e/ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/eltwise/unary_backward/unary_backward.cpp#L1668-L1676)
  — `multiply(reciprocal(input), fill_first_val_into_tensor(prod * grad))`.
- per-dimension: `reciprocal_input` is built once at
  [`L1711`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/a5cd86212e/ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/eltwise/unary_backward/unary_backward.cpp#L1711)
  and feeds every `dim` branch, e.g. `dim=-1` at
  [`L1722`](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/a5cd86212e/ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/eltwise/unary_backward/unary_backward.cpp#L1722).
  All four dimensions are affected, not only `dim=-1`.

At a zero input the product of the other values has already been lost in the reduction, so it
cannot be recovered by the division. The formula is valid only when the reduced input has no zeros.

## Reproducer

Host only, no device required (`pip install torch`):

```python
"""Source-level replay of ttnn.prod_bw against torch.prod autograd.

Replays the composite expression from tt-metal main @ a5cd86212e. Runs on host only:
it does not need a Tenstorrent device.
"""

import math
import torch


def source_prod_bw(values, grad):
    """unary_backward.cpp L1668-1676: reciprocal(input) * broadcast(prod(input) * grad)."""
    product = math.prod(values)
    out = []
    for v in values:
        if v == 0.0:
            # reciprocal(0) is +inf on device; inf * 0 is non-finite
            out.append(float("inf") * (product * grad))
        else:
            out.append(product * grad / v)
    return out


def source_prod_bw_dim(rows, grad):
    """unary_backward.cpp L1711-1722, dim=-1: bcast(reciprocal(input), prod * grad, MUL)."""
    return [source_prod_bw(row, grad) for row in rows]


def torch_prod_bw(values, grad):
    t = torch.tensor(values, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
    torch.prod(t).backward(torch.tensor(grad, dtype=torch.float64))
    return t.grad.tolist()


def torch_prod_bw_dim(rows, grad):
    t = torch.tensor(rows, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
    torch.prod(t, dim=-1, keepdim=True).backward(
        torch.full((len(rows), 1), grad, dtype=torch.float64))
    return t.grad.tolist()


def show(v):
    return "non-finite" if isinstance(v, float) and not math.isfinite(v) else f"{v:g}"


print("dim=None")
for values in ([2.0, 3.0, 4.0], [2.0, 0.0, 4.0], [0.0, 0.0, 4.0], [1.0, 5.0, 0.0]):
    actual, expected = source_prod_bw(values, 1.0), torch_prod_bw(values, 1.0)
    ok = all(a == e for a, e in zip(actual, expected))
    print(f"  input={values}  expected={expected}  "
          f"current=[{', '.join(show(a) for a in actual)}]  {'ok' if ok else 'DIVERGES'}")

print("dim=-1")
for rows in ([[2.0, 3.0, 4.0], [1.0, 5.0, 3.0]], [[2.0, 0.0, 4.0], [1.0, 5.0, 3.0]]):
    actual, expected = source_prod_bw_dim(rows, 1.0), torch_prod_bw_dim(rows, 1.0)
    ok = all(a == e for ar, er in zip(actual, expected) for a, e in zip(ar, er))
    print(f"  input={rows}  expected={expected}  "
          f"current=[{', '.join('[' + ', '.join(show(a) for a in r) + ']' for r in actual)}]  "
          f"{'ok' if ok else 'DIVERGES'}")
```

Output:

```text
dim=None

**Context**
`resolveLilySdkConfig` in `src/config/resolve-config.ts` calls `resolveCredential` unconditionally for `LILY_API_KEY` and `LILY_AUTH_TOKEN`. `resolveCredential` reads `process.env[envName]` with no `typeof process !== 'undefined'` guard, while `resolveBaseUrl` and `LilySdk.create()` in `src/sdk.ts` do guard. The SDK ships a browser build (`dist/browser/`, ES2022, no Node globals per `tsup.config.ts`), but any `new LilySdk({ baseUrl })` or `LilySdk.create({}) ` in a browser throws `ReferenceError: process is not defined` at config resolution, even when no credentials are involved.

**Proposed Change**
Guard the env access in `resolveCredential` (`typeof process === 'undefined' ? undefined : process.env[envName]`) so the resolved config is identical in browsers, and add a regression test that resolves config in an environment without a `process` global.

**Acceptance Criteria**
- `resolveLilySdkConfig({ baseUrl: 'https://api.example.com' })` succeeds with `process` deleted/undefined.
- No `process` reference remains unguarded in `src/config/resolve-config.ts`.
- A regression test simulates the browser environment and asserts both `new LilySdk(...)` and the config resolver work.

**Context**
In `createFetchHttpClient` (`src/http/fetch-http-client.ts`), `parseResponse` runs before the status check. When a server error (e.g. 500) declares `content-type: application/json` but returns an empty or malformed body, `response.json()` rejects and `parseResponse` throws `LilyValidationError` with code `RESPONSE_VALIDATION_ERROR` and status 500; the catch block then rethrows it as a `LilySdkError`. Callers see a confusing "Failed to parse response body as JSON" validation error instead of the actual server failure (`LilyServerError`/appropriate `LilyApiError`), and lose the status-aware handling they'd otherwise get.

**Proposed Change**
Decide JSON handling per status before throwing: keep the strict parse-and-throw `LilyValidationError` for successful (2xx) responses, but for non-ok responses treat an unparseable body as an API failure instead — throw a plain `LilyApiError` carrying the real status code with the raw content-type and the attempted-body text surfaced in `details`, rather than a body-parse validation error. Keep the existing clear error behavior for 2xx responses with empty JSON bodies.

**Acceptance Criteria**
- A 500 response with `content-type: application/json` and an empty body throws a server/API error, not `LilyValidationError`.
- 2xx empty-JSON-body behavior is unchanged.
- Tests cover 204, empty 200 JSON, and empty 500 JSON bodies.

**Suggested Label** (bug)

body_excerpt:
**Component / Area:** ttnn eltwise unary backward (composite), `hardswish_bw`

**Issue Type:** Bad Outputs

## Summary

`hardswish_bw` is composed as
([unary_backward.cpp#L923-L945](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/9fa00fce13cda1538f0130695576408ff5b05665/ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/eltwise/unary_backward/unary_backward.cpp#L923-L945)):

```cpp
where(lt(input, -3.0f), 0.f,
      where(le(input, 3.0f), grad * (input * 0.3333f + 0.5f), grad))
```

PyTorch's reference kernel
([aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/Activation.cpp, hardswish_backward_kernel](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/Activation.cpp))
is

```cpp
if (self <= -3) return 0;
else if (self < 3) return grad * (self / 3 + 0.5);
else return grad;
```

Both boundary comparisons are inverted relative to the reference: ttnn is `<` at -3 where torch is `<=`, and `<=` at +3
where torch is `<`. The registered golden for this op is torch autograd, so the op and its golden disagree at exactly
`x = ±3`. Those values are bf16-exact and ordinary in activation tensors, so exact hits are not rare.

A secondary defect on the same line: the slope constant is `0.3333f` while the forward `hardswish` kernel uses the
correctly rounded `1/6` (`hardsigmoid_init` loads `0.1666666716337204f`). In fp32 this costs 336 to 2097 ULP everywhere in
`(-3, 3)`; at `x = 2.5` the op returns `1.33325` for `1.3333333`.

This is a source-level analysis with a host replay; I do not have a card. The comparisons and constants are exact, so the
device result at `±3` is the same as the replay.

## Observed vs expected (identical in fp32 and bf16, since ±3 is exact in both)

| x | grad | `hardswish_bw` now | torch autograd | abs error |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| -3 | 1 | -0.4999 | 0 | 0.50 |
| +3 | 1 | 1.4999 | 1 | 0.50 |
| -3 | 2 | -0.9998 | 0 | 1.00 |
| +3 | -2 | -2.9998 | -2 | 1.00 |
| 2.5 | 1 | 1.33325 | 1.3333333 | 8.3e-5 |

At `x = -3` the returned gradient even has the wrong sign (negative where the reference is exactly 0).

## Why the tests do not catch it

The nightly test draws inputs from `uniform(-100, 100)` in bf16 and compares by PCC; two wrong lanes out of a
320×384 tensor do not move the PCC, and the sampled inputs rarely land on exactly ±3.

## Reproducer (host only, `pip install torch`)

```python
import torch

def ttnn_hardswish_bw(grad, x):                                   # unary_backward.cpp L923-945
    inner = grad * (x * torch.tensor(0.3333) + 0.5)
    return torch.where(x < -3, torch.tensor(0.0), torch.where(x <= 3, inner, grad))

x = torch.tensor([-3., 3., -3., 3., 2.5], requires_grad=True)
g = torch.tensor([1., 1., 2., -2., 1.])
torch.nn.functional.hardswish(x).backward(g)
print(ttnn_hardswish_bw(g, x.detach()).tolist())   # [-0.4999, 1.4999, -0.9998, -2.9998, 1.33325]
print(x.grad.tolist())                             # [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, -2.0, 1.3333333]
```

## Proposed fix

```cpp
Tensor grad_result = where(
    ttnn::le(input, -3.0f, std::nullopt, output_mem_config),
    0.f,
    where(
        ttnn::lt(input, 3.0f, std::nullopt, output_mem_config),
        ttnn::multiply(grad, ttnn::add(ttnn::multiply(input, 1.0f / 3.0f), 0.5f)),   // 0x3eaaaaab
        grad));
```

Also fix the stale comment above the function, and add `x = ±3` rows (fp32 and bf16) plus an fp32 accuracy check inside
`(-3, 3)` to `test_backward_hardswish.py`.

## Acceptance criteria (proposed)

- `ttnn.hardswish_bw` returns 0 at `x = -3` and `grad` at `x = 3` for fp32 and bf16, matching torch autograd.
- Inside `(-3, 3)` the fp32 result matches `grad * (x / 3 + 0.5)` to a few ULP (no `0.3333f` truncation).
- Nightly test extended with the boundary rows.
title: [Bounty $750] ttnn.hardswish_bw takes the wrong branch at exactly x = ±3 and uses 0.3333 for 1/3

body_excerpt:
**Component / Area:** ttnn eltwise unary backward (composite), `atanh_bw`

**Issue Type:** Bad Outputs

## Summary

`atanh_bw` computes `grad / (1 - x^2)` and then applies

```cpp
grad_a = where(ttnn::eqz(grad), t_nan, grad_a);                       // L972
grad_a = where(logical_and(eqz(grad), eqz(input)), 0.f, grad_a);      // L973-978
```

([unary_backward.cpp#L957-L996](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/9fa00fce13cda1538f0130695576408ff5b05665/ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/eltwise/unary_backward/unary_backward.cpp#L957-L996)).

The first guard was meant to encode `0 * inf = NaN` at the poles `|x| = 1`, but it has no pole condition. The second guard
rescues only `x == 0`. So every position in the open interval `0 < |x| < 1`, which is the entire finite domain of `atanh`,
returns NaN whenever the upstream gradient is exactly zero. Torch returns 0 there and NaN only at `|x| == 1`.

Zero upstream gradients are routine (attention masks, dropout, padded positions, `where` in the graph). One zero in
`grad` poisons the whole backward pass through this op.

This is a source-level analysis with a host replay; I do not have a card. The `where`/`eqz` chain is exact, so the
device result is NaN where the replay says NaN.

## Observed vs expected

| grad | x | `atanh_bw` now | torch `grad / (1 - x^2)` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.5 | **NaN** | 0 |
| 0 | -0.3 | **NaN** | 0 |
| 0 | 0.9 | **NaN** | 0 |
| 0 | 0.25 | **NaN** | 0 |
| 0 | 0.0 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 0.99 | 50.2513 | 50.2513 |
| 0 | 1.0 | NaN | NaN (0 * inf) |

## Why the tests do not catch it

The nightly test
([test_backward_atanh.py](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/9fa00fce13cda1538f0130695576408ff5b05665/tests/ttnn/nightly/unit_tests/operations/eltwise/backward/test_backward_atanh.py))
draws `grad` from `uniform(-100, 100)`, so an exact zero never occurs, and the PCC comparison ignores NaN lanes.

This is distinct from #54695 (the final guard rewriting overflowed `+inf` to `-inf` for negative gradients) and #53884
(dispatch count of the guards).

## Reproducer (host only, `pip install torch`)

```python
import torch
NAN, INF = float("nan"), float("inf")

def ttnn_atanh_bw(grad, x):                                   # unary_backward.cpp L957-996
    ga = grad * (1.0 / (-(x * x - 1.0)))
    ga = torch.where(grad == 0, torch.tensor(NAN), ga)                          # L972
    ga = torch.where((grad == 0) & (x == 0), torch.tensor(0.0), ga)             # L973-978
    ga = torch.where(((x == 1) | (x == -1)) & (grad != 0), torch.tensor(INF), ga)
    return torch.where((ga == INF) & (grad < 0), torch.tensor(-INF), ga)

x = torch.tensor([0.5, -0.3, 0.9, 0.0, 0.99, 0.25])
g = torch.tensor([0., 0., 0., 0., 1., 0.])
xr = x.clone().requires_grad_(True)
torch.atanh(xr).backward(g)
print(ttnn_atanh_bw(g, x).tolist())   # [nan, nan, nan, 0.0, 50.25, nan]
print(xr.grad.tolist())               # [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 50.25, 0.0]
```

## Proposed fix

Make the pole handling explicit and drop the unconditional guard:

```cpp
Tensor grad_a = multiply(grad, unary_chain(input, {SQUARE, SUB_UNARY_SFPU 1.0f, NEG, RECIP}));
Tensor at_pole = logical_or(eq(input, 1.0f), eq(input, -1.0f));
grad_a = where(logical_and(at_pole, eqz(grad)), t_nan, grad_a);                       // 0 * inf
grad_a = where(logical_and(at_pole, nez(grad)), multiply(sign(grad), t_inf), grad_a);  // signed inf at the poles
```

The signed-inf line also resolves #54695, since the overflow rewrite guard is no longer needed. Add a nightly case with
zeros in `grad` (for example a random 50% mask) and an explicit `|x| == 1` row.

## Acceptance criteria (proposed)

- `ttnn.atanh_bw` returns 0 wherever `grad == 0` and `|x| < 1`, matching torch autograd, for fp32 and bf16.
- NaN only where torch produces NaN (`grad == 0` at `|x| == 1`); signed infinity at `|x| == 1` for non-zero `grad`.
- Nightly test extended with a masked gradient and the pole rows.
title: [Bounty $1,000] ttnn.atanh_bw returns NaN for every element whose upstream gradient is exactly zero

body_excerpt:
**Component / Area:** ttnn eltwise unary backward (composite), `rpow_bw`

**Issue Type:** Bad Outputs

## Summary

`ttnn.rpow(x, base)` is `base ** x`: the SFPU kernel says so
([ckernel_sfpu_rpow.h#L12](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/9fa00fce13cda1538f0130695576408ff5b05665/tt_metal/hw/ckernels/blackhole/metal/llk_api/llk_sfpu/ckernel_sfpu_rpow.h#L12),
`// ttnn.rpow(exponent, scalar_base) = pow(scalar_base, exponent)`) and the forward golden is `torch.pow(dim, input_tensor_a)`
([unary.py#L812-L818](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/9fa00fce13cda1538f0130695576408ff5b05665/ttnn/ttnn/operations/unary.py#L812-L818)).

`ttnn.rpow_bw` returns `grad * base * x**(base-1)`, which is the derivative of `x ** base`
([unary_backward.cpp#L802-L817](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/9fa00fce13cda1538f0130695576408ff5b05665/ttnn/cpp/ttnn/operations/eltwise/unary_backward/unary_backward.cpp#L802-L817)).
The correct derivative of `base ** x` is `base**x * ln(base)`. The two agree only at `x == 1`. Because `x**(base-1)` is
undefined for negative `x` with a non-integer `base`, the op also forces NaN for every `x < 0`, where `base ** x` is an
ordinary finite number.

```cpp
// unary_backward.cpp L802-817 (paraphrased)
grad_result = zeros_like(input);
if (exponent != 0) {
    grad_result = grad * (pow(input, exponent - 1) * exponent);   // d/dx x^exponent
    grad_result = where(ltz(input), NaN, grad_result);
}
```

This is a source-level analysis with a host replay; I do not have a card. The host replay reproduces the composition in
float32 torch; the device numbers will differ only by the usual ULP-level SFPU error, not in kind.

## Observed vs expected (grad = 1, fp32)

| base | x | `rpow_bw` now | correct `base**x * ln(base)` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.0 | -1.0 | **NaN** | 0.3466 |
| 2.0 | 0.0 | 0 | 0.6931 |
| 2.0 | 2.0 | 4.0 | 2.7726 |
| 2.0 | 3.0 | 6.0 | 5.5452 |
| 5.7 | 3.0 | 996.2 | 322.3 |
| 15.2 | 2.0 | 286068 | 628.7 |
| 15.2 | 0.5 | 0.0008 | 10.61 |

## Why the tests do not catch it

The registered backward golden replicates the same misreading:
[unary_backward.py#L197-L202](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/9fa00fce13cda1538f0130695576408ff5b05665/ttnn/ttnn/operations/unary_backward.py#L197-L202)
calls `_golden_function_unary_backward_with_float("pow", grad, input, alpha)`, i.e. autograd of `torch.pow(input, alpha)`
(`input ** alpha`). The nightly test
([test_backward_rpow.py](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/blob/9fa00fce13cda1538f0130695576408ff5b05665/tests/ttnn/nightly/unit_tests/operations/eltwise/backward/test_backward_rpow.py))
and the sweep golden compare only against that, so the op and its golden agree with each other and both disagree with the
forward op's own golden.

## Reproducer (host only, `pip install torch`)

```python
import torch

def ttnn_rpow_bw(grad, x, base):            # unary_backward.cpp L802-817
    if base == 0.0:
        return torch.zeros_like(x)
    r = grad * (torch.pow(x, base - 1.0) * base)
    return torch.where(x < 0, torch.tensor(float("nan")), r)

x = torch.tensor([-2., -1., 0., 0.5, 1., 2., 3.])
g = torch.ones_like(x)
for base in (1.5, 2.0, 5.7, 15.2):
    xr = x.clone().requires_grad_(True)
    torch.pow(base, xr).backward(g)         # autograd of the forward op's golden, torch.pow(base, x)
    print(base, ttnn_rpow_bw(g, x, base).tolist(), xr.grad.tolist())
```

## Proposed fix

```cpp
// d/dx base^x = base^x * ln(base). Forward docs already state non-positive bases are unsupported.
Tensor result = ttnn::multiply(grad, ttnn::rpow(input, exponent, output_mem_config), std::nullopt, output_mem_config);
result = ttnn::multiply(result, std::log(exponent), std::nullopt, output_mem_config);
```

Keep the `exponent == 0` zeros path (matches `torch.pow(0., x)` autograd for `x > 0`). Change the backward golden and the
sweep golden to autograd of `torch.pow(alpha, input)`, and add `x < 0` and `x == 0` rows to the nightly test so the
regression is pinned.
title: [Bounty $1,000] ttnn.rpow_bw computes the gradient of x**base instead of base**x; NaN for every negative input

**Context**
`HealthStatus` in `src/models/system.ts` declares `status`, `version: string`, `timestamp: string`, and `checks: Record<string, 'ok'|'degraded'|'down'>` as required fields. `validateHealthStatus` in `src/validation/health-status.ts` (used by `SystemClient.health` when `validateResponses` is enabled) validates a different shape: it only requires `status`, treats `version` as optional, validates an `uptime` number field that does not exist on the model, and never validates `timestamp` or `checks`. The validator also returns `HealthStatusShape` which `SystemClient.health` casts away with `as unknown as HealthStatus`, so the drift is invisible to callers until a malformed payload slips through.

**Proposed Change**
Decide the authoritative wire shape for `GET /v1/system/health` and align the model type, the validator, and the tests. Either remove `timestamp`/`checks` from `HealthStatus` and keep `uptime` if the backend returns uptime, or extend `validateHealthStatus` to require/validate `timestamp` and `checks` and drop `uptime`. Update `tests/health-status-validation.test.ts` and `tests/health-validation.test.ts` accordingly and remove the unsafe double cast.

**Acceptance Criteria**
- `HealthStatus` (src/models/system.ts) and `validateHealthStatus` validate the same required and optional fields.
- A payload with a malformed `timestamp` or `checks` entry is rejected when validation is enabled.
- `uptime` is either removed from the validator or added to the model type.
- `SystemClient.health` no longer needs `as unknown as HealthStatus`.

**Suggested Label** (bug)

**ETA:** 24 hours
title: [Bounty: $85] Reconcile HealthStatus model type with the validateHealthStatus validator

# 📰 ArXiv AI 研究日报（2026-09-03）

## 一、今日速览

今日 50 篇 AI 相关论文中，**LLM 后训练与推理增强**仍是绝对主线：包括竞赛编程金牌级别的端到端特化管线（#9）、从“第一个错误”学习过程奖励的 Cliff（#13），以及多项针对长上下文注意力效率的创新（#33、#41）。**智能体安全与评估**方向密集出现，SafeEvolve 提出安全策略与 harness 协同进化，EarlyEval 和 CodePoisonRAG 分别从评估成本和 RAG 投毒攻击切入。**极致低精度与压缩**持续升温：FP4 预训练配方、Leech 格 2-bit 权重解码均有新进展。理论侧也有关键突破——梯度下降下界首次超越经典 Nesterov 界限。

---

## 二、重点论文

### 🧠 大语言模型（架构、训练、对齐、评估）

**1. Post-Training Language Models for Gold-Medal Performance in Coding Competitions**
- 链接：http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02849v1 | Ficek, Narenthiran, Samadi et al.
- 端到端竞赛编程特化管线（大规模题目收集 + 合成推理轨迹），冲击 IOI/ICPC 金牌水平，是 LLM 推理后训练的代表性工作。

**2. Cliff: Learning Process Rewards from the First Mistake**
- 链接：http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02817v1 | Han, Wang, Ramaneti et al.
- 从推理轨迹中“第一个错误”处截断学习过程奖励，为 RLVR 提供细粒度中间监督，突破粗粒度 outcome reward 的瓶颈。

**3. Language Models Can Control Their Own Attention**
- 链接：http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02737v1 | Ho, Ahmad, Koh et al.
- 让模型学会主动控制自身注意力、避免全 KV cache 扫描，直击超长上下文（1M token）推理效率痛点。

**4. Trace as State: Reasoning Traces as Conditional States for Long-Context Transformers**
- 链接：http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02702v1 | Zou, Tang
- 形式化“条件状态更新”任务，证明先给出条件可使最坏情况内存需求从指数级降低，为长上下文架构设计提供理论指引。

**5. UE5M3 FP4 Block Scaling for Stable Language Model Pretraining**
- 链接：http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02846v1 | Hu, Luschi, Balanca
- 提出比 NVIDIA TE recipe 更轻量的 FP4 块缩放方案，推动 4-bit 稳定预训练走向实用。

**6. User Feedback Provides a Unique Signal that LLMs Can not Detect**
- 链接：http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02859v1 | Don-Yehiya, Choshen, Abend
- 证明用户反馈包含 LLM 自身无法检测的独特学习信号，挑战“用户反馈噪声大、难利用”的固有认知。

**7. The Implications of Linguistic Illegibility for LLM Security**
- 链接：http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02852v1 | Mickens
- 提出“语言学不可读性”概念：模型外部语言输出并非内部计算的可靠透镜，对可解释性与安全审计有深刻警示意义。

**8. Improved Gradient Descent Lower Bounds Beyond Nesterov**
- 链接：http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02855v1 | Ye, Liu
- 首次超越经典 Ω(n⁻²) 一阶下界，证明 Ω(n⁻¹·⁶³⁴²) 非随时下界，优化理论重要进展。

### 🤖 智能体与推理（规划、工具使用、多智能体、安全）

**9. SafeEvolve: Harness-Policy Co-Evolution from Agent Experience for Safety Alignment**
- 链接：http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02786v1 | Mao, Qu, Guo et al.
- 提出安全 harness 与模型策略基于智能体经验的协同进化，覆盖多步执行轨迹中的安全风险。

**10. EarlyEval: Cheaper Agent Evaluation via Early Outcome Prediction**
- 链接：http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02783v1 | Shi, Sun, Dong et al.
- 通过早期结果预测大幅削减智能体评估成本（单次基准跑动辄数百至数千美元），直击迭代开发的经济瓶颈。

**11. Discriminative World Models for Web Agents**
- 链接：http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02885v1 | Li, Pendharkar, Pahilajani et al.
- 用判别式（而非生成式 next-state 预测）世界模型改进 Web 智能体测试时动作选择。

**12. Bilevel Coordinated Reflection: A Game-Theoretic Approach to Multi-Agent LLM Systems**
- 链接：http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02750v1 | Chen, Chen, Huang et al.
- 用博弈论双层结构统一刻画多智能体 LLM 系统的协调、记忆改进与外部验证角色。

**13. Repo-To-Skill: Distilling GitHub Repositories Into AI4AI Skills**
- 链接：http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02749v1 | Chen, Hu, Qian et al.
- 将 GitHub 仓库蒸馏为可复用的“操作技能”层，补齐自主 ML 研究智能体缺失的领域专有知识。

### 🔧 方法与框架（新技术、基准、效率优化）

On 23 August, Surya Narreddi posted a beautiful video of watercolours painted by a language model. The model writes JavaScript through p5.brush, a library that "adds natural drawing tools to p5.js". The video went viral fast, over 1.5M views at the time of writing.
The video came with a blog post explaining the training behind an earlier and narrower stage of the project, close-up flowers rather than the full compositions in the video, sadly without open artifacts yet. His site says a full technical report is coming, so ensure you follow him. The original idea is his, coming from the art and design side, where his skills are way beyond mine. My attempt is on the engineering side, reproducing the recipe in the open with every piece published.
Note: for the context behind the project, told by Surya himself, watch this video of his thesis.
In this article I try and reproduce his idea with TRL and OpenEnv. The reference pool dataset, the RL environment, the training scripts and the trained models, all open.
The whole pipeline runs on Hugging Face, end to end:
- training on Jobs
- the RL environment and the scorer model as Spaces
- the pairwise judge through Inference Providers
- and every artifact on the Hub, gathered in one collection
Once the two Spaces are up, the recipe is one command. Duplicate the environment and the scorer model, set two environment variables for the reward mix, and launch:
hf jobs uv run train/watercolour_grpo.py --flavor h200 --timeout 48h --secrets HF_TOKEN -- \
  --env-url https://<you>-watercolour-env.hf.space \
  --model Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B --lora --all-linear --bf16 --gradient-checkpointing \
  --subject 'a peach hibiscus' --references 4 \
  --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 \
  --lr 5e-5 --lr-scheduler constant_with_warmup --warmup-steps 5 \
  --scale-rewards none \
  --steps 110 --n-episodes 240 --num-generations 8 \
  --per-device-batch-size 1 --gradient-accumulation-steps 8 \
  --max-completion-length 8192 \
  --run-tag my-run --out <you>/watercolour-grpo --push-to-hub
The rest of this article is the story of getting there, and every piece is in the repo.
I have followed the original blog step by step, and only changed something when strictly needed. Every idea of my own went into a list instead of into the experiment, and that list became "What I would try next" at the end, next to the full list of published artifacts. If you have already read his post, the framing and the reward design will be familiar. The new material is the open implementation, the hand-rated pool, and three reward mixes trained and compared, and it starts at The RL environment you need to build.
The paintings look loose, imperfect, handmade, at a moment when image models produce perfect (statistically average) pictures. My guess is that this contrast is a big part of why the video went viral. It reminded me of the early days of generative AI art, when the point was to explore the medium. DeepDream (2015) was a debugging tool that people turned into art, works like Edmond de Belamy (2018) came from artists probing what a GAN could do, and artists like Mario Klingemann spent those ye
