## Summary

#3149 ended by naming its own next step:

> *"Next step is to establish which of those two directions the block copier is running in per
> dispatch — input detile or result re-tile — and whether a dispatch whose result is unchanged still
> pays for it."*

**It is the result re-tile**, and it is 61% of compute-image writeback time.

## Measured

Stray title screen (`PPSA02101`), `origin/main` `fc21d46ca`, `reach-title-hold.pad`,
`PROSPER_NULL_PAGE=1`, 3840x2160, `PROSPER_COMPUTE_IMAGE_TIMING=1`. Aggregated over **4,291
`[compute-image-writeback]` records**:

| stage | total | share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`layout_ms`** | **2794.2 ms** | **61%** |
| **`watch_ms`** | **1417.1 ms** | **31%** |
| `cache_ms` | 286.7 ms | 6% |
| `pack_ms` | 66.0 ms | 1% |
| `notify_ms` / `map_ms` / `prepare_ms` | 17.4 ms | ~0% |
| total | 4584.6 ms | |

By program:

| program | writeback total | n | mean |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `0x30112e0000` | 1405.2 ms | 325 | 4.324 ms |
| `0x300bc70000` | 1230.1 ms | 976 | 1.260 ms |
| `0x3011300000` | 1228.1 ms | 321 | 3.826 ms |
| `0x300dfa0000` | 620.1 ms | 648 | 0.957 ms |

`layout_ms` is the span from `pack_done` to `layout_done` at `live_compute.cpp:10085-10115` — the
`tile_surface` / `tile_surface_level` calls that convert the linear compute result **back into the
guest's tiled layout**. That is the `parallel_rows<sw64kb_copy<...>>` and `__memmove_avx512` cost
#3149 saw in `perf`, now attributed to a direction and a stage.

## Why this is worth acting on

The title screen renders at **9.76 fps** (F8 capture, 5.02 s window at t=175 s). `gpu-device` is
232.5 ms of that window — **~5%** — so the GPU is idle and the frame is host-bound. Compute is
1981.5 ms and renderer-resource 1895.5 ms, i.e. two nearly equal halves rather than one hot spot.

`watch_ms` at 31% is the second target and has had no attention: that is guest-write-watch
registration per writeback, and #3155's promotion machinery already exists for compute *buffers*.

## Two directions, neither yet tested

1. **Skip the re-tile when the result is unchanged.** `live_compute.cpp:9019` already computes
   `changed_bytes` against the seed and `__memcmp_evex_movbe` was 1.4% of CPU in #3149's profile, so
   the detector is already being paid for. What is not established is how often a Stray writeback is
   actually unchanged — if it is rare, this buys nothing.
2. **Avoid the round trip.** A result that is re-tiled into guest memory and then re-uploaded for the
   next dispatch has made a CPU round trip for nothing. Whether that is the pattern here is not
   established either.

## Instrument caveat, stated rather than buried

`PROSPER_COMPUTE_IMAGE_TIMING` adds per-writeback clock reads and logging, so the **absolute** figures
come from a perturbed run and are an upper bound on a default one. The *stage attribution* does not
depend on that: `layout_ms` brackets real `tile_surface` work between two clock reads, and the 61/31
split is a ratio within the same instrumented run. Re-measure absolutes with F8 before quoting one as
a default-run number.

Related: #3149 (closed, splash-phase measurement), #3126 (Stray title screen), #3155 (write-watch
promotion for buffers).
title: Compute-image writeback is 61% CPU re-tiling and 31% write-watch registration — answering #3149's open question

WGC + CEF + NVENC load, endurance, restart/crash recovery, runtime coexistence, saturation, lease/mapping recovery and rollback.

## Severity
**High**

## Summary
The README's "Community reward engine" section states, in the present tense, that the product currently shows this to visitors:

> "The interface now displays a **5M ARCHITECTURE reward pool** and a **10% bounty allocation**."

and

> "Current revenue policy displayed by the project: **10% → ARCHITECTURE buybacks**, **10% → community bounties**"

None of this exists on the live homepage (`https://grok-architecture.com/`). There is no reward-pool figure, no bounty-allocation percentage, and no revenue-split display anywhere in the rendered page.

## Evidence
- Live DOM check on `https://www.grok-architecture.com/`: zero elements matching `[class*="bounty"]`, and no page text matching `5M`, `reward pool`, or `bounty`.
- `styles.css` still contains a full set of unused rules for this feature that has no corresponding markup in `index.html`: `.bounty-pool-card`, `.bounty-kicker`, `.bounty-main`, `.bounty-meta`, `.bounty-dialog`, `.bounty-allocation`, `.routing-row.buyback`, `.routing-row.bounty`, etc. This strongly suggests the feature was built, then removed from the shipped UI, without the README being updated to match.
- `index.html` and `app.js` contain no references to "bounty", "reward pool", or a revenue-split display.

## Reproduction
1. Open https://grok-architecture.com/ (desktop or mobile) and read through the entire visible page.
2. Search for any mention of a reward pool size, bounty allocation percentage, or buyback/bounty revenue split — none is present.
3. Compare against README.md's "Community reward engine" section, which describes this as a current, live feature ("now displays...").

## Impact
The README is the primary reference a new user, contributor, or holder will read to understand what the product currently does. Describing a live UI element that isn't there erodes trust and could be read as tokenomics presented as build/product when it doesn't actually exist yet — a serious ambiguity for a project trading a real token.

## Recommended fix
Either:
1. Ship the reward-pool/bounty-allocation UI described (the CSS is already in place, so only markup + data wiring may be needed), or
2. Edit the README to move this section into "Development path" (future work) instead of describing it as currently live, until it actually ships.
title: [High] README describes a 5M reward pool / bounty allocation UI that does not exist on the live site

## Severity
**Critical**

## Summary
The README's "Community reward engine" section instructs the community to post the token contract address for bounty-qualifying content, and gives this address:

```
AP8Wnu37Gf9RHgugPKGvpHe6LcTE2yp5GDy7pL5Upump
```

This is a Solana/pump.fun-style address. However, the actual live `$GBA` token used everywhere in the shipped product (main site, Holder HQ, DexScreener widget, Pons launchpad link, on-chain explorer) is a completely different, EVM-style address on "Robinhood Chain":

```
0xe2f888673ab2467146e33f079fdb7be09285d5da
```

## Evidence
- README.md, "Community reward engine" section: lists `AP8Wnu37Gf9RHgugPKGvpHe6LcTE2yp5GDy7pL5Upump`.
- `app.js` (live site): `const TOKEN_ADDRESS = '0xe2f888673ab2467146e33f079fdb7be09285d5da';` — used for the DexScreener price feed and the Pons launchpad link.
- `https://www.architecture-holders.com/` ("Holder HQ"): displays contract `0xe2f888673ab2467146e33f079fdb7be09285d5da`, network "ROBINHOOD CHAIN", with working "COPY CA", Pons, and block-explorer links all pointing at this same EVM address.
- DexScreener API confirms this EVM address is the live, traded `$GBA` pair: `https://api.dexscreener.com/latest/dex/tokens/0xe2f888673ab2467146e33f079fdb7be09285d5da`.

## Reproduction
1. Open `README.md` and find the contract address under "Community reward engine" (`AP8Wnu37Gf9RHgugPKGvpHe6LcTE2yp5GDy7pL5Upump`).
2. Open https://www.architecture-holders.com/ and read the "CONTRACT" field: `0xe2f888673ab2467146e33f079fdb7be09285d5da`.
3. Compare — the two addresses are unrelated and on different chains/formats.

## Impact
Anyone following the README to submit bounty evidence, or verifying which token is "official," is told to reference a token address that does not match the one actually traded, tracked, and paid out against. This is exactly the kind of inconsistency that gets a project accused of running a copycat/scam token, and it actively risks real financial harm to community members who buy or reference the wrong contract.

## Recommended fix
Update the README's "Community reward engine" section to use the correct, live `$GBA` contract address (`0xe2f888673ab2467146e33f079fdb7be09285d5da` on Robinhood Chain), or clarify explicitly if `AP8Wnu37Gf9RHgugPKGvpHe6LcTE2yp5GDy7pL5Upump` is an intentionally separate/legacy token — in which case the README must say so unambiguously, since as written it reads as the same product's token.
title: [Critical] Contract address mismatch: README bounty section vs. live token ($GBA)

# Goal

Track the **post-B2 machine-learning program** for the locked Akiri, Fearless Voyager vs. Chevill, Bane of Monsters Commander curriculum after `DATA_TRUSTED=YES`.

This roadmap refines the existing high-level sequence:

```text
C0 ML Strategy
→ C1 Teacher / Bootstrap
→ C2 Recurrent RL
→ C3 Self-Play
→ C4 Generalization
```

It does **not** renumber the accepted roadmap and does **not** authorize implementation, training, RL, self-play, hierarchy, search, world models, curriculum expansion, or deck changes by itself.

Authoritative environment/data gate:

- #100 — B2 Trusted Commander Trajectory V1 contract and replay-backed dataset gate

Core principle remains:

```text
DO NOT TRAIN ON AN ENVIRONMENT WE DO NOT TRUST.
```

Entry requirement:

```text
B2 FINAL_ACCEPTANCE_PASS=YES
DATA_TRUSTED=YES
```

Until then:

```text
C0_AUTHORIZED=NO
TRAINING_AUTHORIZED=NO
```

---

# Non-negotiable ML boundary

The policy sample remains:

```text
PlayerObservationV1
+ complete currently legal candidate/domain
+ chosen semantic action/response
```

The engine remains the sole authority for:

- Magic rules;
- legal actions / structured domains;
- perspective-safe observations;
- replay/determinism;
- factual episode closure;
- exact environment transition.

The model may score or reason over currently supplied legal choices, but must never:

- invent legal actions;
- repair or truncate candidate/domain sets;
- replace complete legal domains with a fixed global action vocabulary;
- reinterpret hidden information as fact;
- expose raw `GameState`;
- make a learned world model authoritative for rules or legality;
- turn search/model belief into a hidden-state oracle.

Preferred action shape remains variable-domain candidate scoring:

```text
public recurrent/history state h_t
+ complete current legal candidates A_t[]
→ score every supplied legal candidate
→ select exactly one current legal action/response
```

---

# Core architecture hypothesis

Long-term hypothesis:

```text
PERSPECTIVE-SAFE OBSERVATION
+ RECURRENT PUBLIC-HISTORY MEMORY
+ VARIABLE-SIZE LEGAL-CANDIDATE SCORING
+ VALUE ESTIMATION
+ OPTIONAL LATENT TEMPORAL HIERARCHY
+ OPTIONAL PLANNING / SEARCH
```

The important ownership split is:

```text
Recurrent memory
→ past public history/context

Value
→ long-horizon estimate

Latent hierarchy
→ persistent strategic intent

World model / search
→ possible future estimates

Argentum
→ reality, rules, legality, actual transition
```

These components are introduced **staged**, not all at once.

---

# C0 — ML Strategy and causal baselines

C0 should decide experiments, not prematurely crown an algorithm.

Before training, freeze at minimum:

- model-facing observation contract;
- candidate/domain encoding contract;
- episode/sequence derivation contract;
- train/validation/test split semantics;
- checkpoint/content identity;
- deterministic inference requirements;
- policy RNG/numeric execution contract where relevant;
- evaluation matrix;
- value/reward ownership boundaries;
- bootstrap/Teacher provenance;
- failure/quarantine behavior.

Do not preselect PPO, R2D2, IMPALA, APPO, AWR, ExIt, MuZero, HRL, or another family merely because it is popular.

---

# Sequence/data contract before recurrent training

Trajectory V1 remains the immutable authoritative episodic source.

Do **not** rewrite canonical trajectories to store framework-specific recurrent windows, burn-in tensors, padding, or hidden-state blobs.

Instead define a deterministic derived recurrent view:

```text
TrajectoryV1
→ sequence derivation contract
→ recurrent training windows / masks / burn-in
```

At minimum preserve:

```text
semanticEpisodeId / trajectoryId
decisionIndex
observationBefore
complete legal domain
chosen semantic action/response
previous accepted semantic action/response where needed
episode closure
sequence start/end
window start/end
burn-in semantics
padding/mask semantics
hidden-state reset semantics
```

ID: STORAGE-001

Status: **PLANNED — FIRST-PLAYABLE BASE LOGISTICS / IMPLEMENTATION WIP=0**
Priority: P1 under #586 after canonical Building/container foundations are accepted/usable
Category: Gameplay / Storage / Building / Persistence / Logistics
First Playable authority: #586
Inventory/container foundation: accepted #208 + downstream canonical Inventory transaction authority
Building definition/instance/runtime: #490/#493/#495
Building interaction/presentation: #407/#416 as applicable
Persistence: accepted SAVE/WorldDelta architecture
Scale: #369

## Why this card exists

The repository has an accepted generic Inventory/container foundation (#208), but the First Playable requires an actual **persistent world storage object** for the Overworld home and Hell Entrance outpost. Audit found no dedicated gameplay owner for a player-built Wooden Chest/container lifecycle.

This card owns one minimal storage object family and its semantic access/persistence contract. It does not create a warehouse framework or global magical inventory.

Core rule:

> **A storage chest is a persistent world object with its own canonical container state. Runtime meshes/UI are disposable views of that semantic state.**

---

# 1. First content scope

Exactly one ordinary storage family is sufficient for V1:
- Wooden Storage Chest / equivalent Biome-1 Wood construction;
- one authored finite slot capacity, exact count tuning later;
- normal stack/instance rules from #208;
- no backpack/upgraded chest/iron chest/magical storage tier required.

The chest may be represented as a BuildDefinition/BuildInstance capability or an equivalent canonical placed-world object using accepted Building identity. Do not create a parallel placement/persistence system merely because it owns Inventory state.

---

# 2. Semantic identity and ownership

Every committed chest has:
- one stable world/build instance identity;
- one stable semantic container identity derived/associated deterministically with that placed object;
- canonical container contents independent from runtime Node identity;
- bounded access/permission metadata sufficient for current single-player and future player-aware multiplayer semantics.

Do not use scene-tree path, runtime instance ID, mesh index or array order as durable container identity.

Deleting/destroying the chest must have an explicit content-disposition policy; never silently delete items through runtime teardown.

First recommendation when a non-empty chest is deliberately deconstructed/destroyed:
- reject deliberate deconstruction until emptied, or
- emit an exact persistent spill/cache transaction under one explicit owner.

Choose one bounded V1 policy before implementation; do not drop contents accidentally because the presentation Node disappeared.

---

# 3. Interaction

Open/close is a world interaction plus ordinary storage UI session.

Conceptual flow:

```text
resolve exact accessible chest
-> open container session/read model
-> player Inventory <-> chest transfer intents
-> canonical atomic Inventory/container transactions
-> refresh value-only UI state
```

UI never owns the container contents.

Required basic operations may include:
- move one stack/item;
- quick transfer;
- stack into compatible existing stacks;
- take all / stack-all only if current UI architecture supports them cleanly.

Do not make sophisticated sorting/filters a correctness requirement.

---

# 4. Persistence / streaming

Container state is durable gameplay truth.

Requirements:
- unload/re-entry retains exact contents;
- Save/Continue reconstructs exact slots/stacks/copy identity according to accepted codecs;
- inactive world/domain need not retain a live chest Node or Inventory object per chest;
- reopening reconstructs/attaches a current runtime view from semantic state;
- stale runtime UI/session handles cannot mutate a destroyed/replaced chest;
- world/domain transition does not duplicate containers or contents.

Do not serialize UI-open state, sele
title: STORAGE-001 — Persistent player-built world containers and bounded local storage access

body_excerpt:
A node can still be OOMKilled after the #413 fix, from a different path: the decentralized-party read fans out one ACS read per hosted party and runs them all at once, holding every result until the last one finishes. Hit this on devnet node 2 today, on the #413 fix, while the other mesh members were restarting: memory went 98Mi to 1614Mi in about 90 seconds and the pod was OOMKilled at its 2Gi limit.

This is **not** a regression of #413 and not the same shape. #413 was one read materializing a whole ACS before filtering; that fix is deployed and holds (node 1 went from OOMKilled-at-4Gi to 23Mi steady, sweeps completing). This is N reads alive concurrently.

## Cause

`fetch_decentralized_parties` (crates/decman/src/server/handlers/parties.rs:771) builds one future per party this participant hosts and awaits them together:

```rust
let futures: Vec<_> = my_parties.into_iter().map(|(item, my_owner_key, p2p)| { ... }).collect();
let results = futures::future::join_all(futures).await;   // :973
```

There is no concurrency limit. Each future does a token fetch, a `get_contracts` ACS read (`queries.rs:230`, returns `Vec<ContractInfo>`) and a `get_party_metadata` call, joined per party. So peak is roughly `hosted parties x per-party ACS result`, all resident at once, and nothing is released until `join_all` returns — `parties` then holds every result for `store_parties_to_db`.

devnet nodes host 213 to 221 parties, so that is 213 concurrent ACS reads.

## Why the mesh churn made it fire

The startup task (crates/decman/src/server/mod.rs:1118, 5s after boot) runs the fan-out and then `resolve_owner_keys_from_peers` (`parties.rs:211`), which dials every peer in turn. A slow or unreachable peer stretches the window, and the per-party futures log nothing unless they fail — which matches what the pod showed: silent, pegged at its 500m CPU limit, climbing, with the last log line a `RequestOwnerKeys` timeout.

Once the mesh settled, the same pod ran flat at 208-209Mi through 18 reward sweeps. So it is the concurrent fan-out under a stretched window, not steady-state load.

## Callers

- crates/decman/src/server/mod.rs:1126 — startup sync, every boot
- crates/decman/src/server/handlers/parties.rs:141 and :188 — the parties endpoints, so a UI read triggers the same fan-out on demand
- crates/decman/src/server/handlers/workflows.rs:1769 and :2309 — background workflow tasks

The on-demand callers matter as much as startup: two overlapping requests double the peak.

## Evidence

* `lastState.terminated`: `OOMKilled`, exit 137, on the #413 fix image
* 98Mi -> 410Mi -> 671Mi -> 1097Mi -> 1138Mi -> 1614Mi sampled over ~90s, ~450m CPU against a 500m limit
* log silent from `Cached 213 decentralized parties from Canton` until the kill
* same pod, mesh settled: 208Mi flat, 6m CPU, restarts 0

## Fix

Bound the fan-out instead of `join_all` — `futures::stream::iter(..).buffer_unordered(N)` with a small N, or a semaphore — so peak tracks N rather than the hosted-party count. Two things worth settling alongside it:

* whether the startup sync needs `contracts` at all, since it only caches parties and then resolves owner keys
* whether the per-party result can be written to the DB as it arrives rather than collected into one `Vec` first

Raising the memory limit is not a workaround here: it scales with hosted parties, and on devnet the PV pins each pod to one zone, where there was no room for 4Gi.
title: Party read OOMs the node: one ACS read per hosted party, all concurrent

## Anlass
Der Live-Check am 20.08.2026 zeigt für Baden-Württemberg auf `/laender/baden-wuerttemberg/mandat-und-praxis` nur die verifizierte Mandatsbasis. Die Seite sagt selbst: `vollständige Commitment-Zerlegung wird fortlaufend ergänzt`.

Der kanonische WÖk-Bestand bestätigt die Fachlücke:
- `/WOEK/WOEK-LAENDER-DAILY/BASELINE/baden-wuerttemberg/BASELINE-2026-08-18.md`: offene Aufgabe `Koalitionsvertrag vollständig in CoalitionCommitments zerlegen`.
- `/WOEK/WOEK-LAENDER-DAILY/CONTROL/LAENDER-COVERAGE-AND-HANDOFF-FINAL-2026-08-18.md`: Koalitionsvertrag 2026-2031 nur `als Mandatsbasis vorgesehen`.
- `/WOEK/WOEK-LAENDER-DAILY/FACHREVIEW/baden-wuerttemberg/INITIAL-IMPACT-CASES-2026-08-18.md`: fünf initiale Regierungswirkungsfälle, aber keine vollständige Koalitionsvertrags-Wirkungsanalyse.

Aktuelle Production ist nicht stale: `dpl_6CefNPFgRYrVXzYTFZeEezsArEX2`, READY/production, Git SHA `fb07fab799a34bbda0e2efc03f90066945c95802`, entsprechend aktuellem main-Basisstand von PR #235. Das BW-Problem ist daher nach aktuellem Befund keine bloße falsche Vercel-Promotion, sondern eine echte fachliche/Publikations-Coverage-Lücke - vorbehaltlich historischem Restore-Fund.

## Rollen
Human out of loop. **CodeX ist technischer Ausführungs- und Deployment-Aktor.** WÖk/Controller liefert Fachbestand, Priorität, Audit und exact-commit Freigabe. CodeX implementiert, testet, merged und deployt bis Production, sobald die Gates grün sind. Kein zusätzliches Human-Gate.

## P0-1 Baden-Württemberg: Restore-first
Vor Neuanalyse Git-Historie, Branches und kanonischen `/WOEK`-Bestand nach einer früher bereits fachlich freigegebenen Koalitionsvertragsanalyse durchsuchen. Wenn vorhanden: exakt/provenienzgebunden wiederherstellen. Keine Neufassung, die einen vorhandenen historischen Fachstand still ersetzt.

Wenn keine vollständige freigegebene Analyse existiert, ist die Fachlücke ausdrücklich zu schließen: amtlichen Koalitionsvertrag 2026-2031 vollständig sichern/versionieren, Commitments mit Source Locator extrahieren und dem WÖk-Fachreview zuführen. CodeX erzeugt **keine** Wirkungsurteile selbst.

## P0-2 Vollständigkeitsaudit alle 16 Länder
Für jedes Land getrennt inventarisieren und öffentlich korrekt abbilden:
- `election_cycle_state` und `government_lifecycle_state` - strikt getrennte Achsen,
- ElectionDocuments/Wahlprogramme und freigegebene Programmanalysen,
- Koalitions-/Mandatsdokumente und Coalition-/MandateCommitments,
- GovernmentActions und WÖkImpactCases,
- AnalysisVersions/RecommendationVersions,
- EvidenceEvents/RealityChecks,
- Quellen, Kompetenz, höherrangiges Recht/Schutzgrenzen,
- öffentliche Routen, Navigation, Overview-Projektion und Detailakten.

Fehlende Fachlayer nicht technisch erfinden. Vorhandenen Fachbestand niemals verkürzen oder verstecken.

## P0-3 Übersicht: Wirkungspotenzial klar sichtbar
Portalweit auf Wahlprogramm-, Koalitions-/Mandats-, Regierungs-, Parlament-, EU- und Länderübersichten muss die WÖk-Einordnung vor Prozessmetadaten verständlich sichtbar sein. Soweit fachlich freigegeben mindestens:
- qualitativer Wirkungspotenzialbefund,
- stärkste positive Potenziale,
- wichtigste materielle Risiken/Zielkonflikte,
- Evidenz/Unsicherheit getrennt von Richtung,
- Richtungsprofil nur für redaktionell/fachlich geprüfte Pfade,
- Nichtkompensation/Schutzgrenzen,
- **alle** freigegebenen Key Findings - keine `slice(0,2)`-Verkürzung,
- keine Partei-/Regierungs-Gesamtnote oder künstliche Saldierung.

Detailseiten müssen die vollständige freigegebene Fachakte und Quellen enthalten, nicht nur Mandats-/Fakten-Teaser.

## P0-4 Golden-State / kein Datenverlust durch Release
Jeder Kandidat gegen letzten akzeptierten Production-Stand **und** kanonischen `/WOEK`-Fachbestand prüfen:
- vorhandene Routen/Navigation,
- Fachakten/Analyseachsen,
- `required_content_paths` vs. `rendered_content_paths`, Pflichtbestand `unrendered_content_paths=[]`,
- Wirkungspotenzial/Key Findings/Wirkpfade/Evidenz,
- Kompetenz/Higher Law/Schutzgrenzen,
- Rec

**Ticket** `BL-01` · **Milestone** Day 4 — Deploy & Submit · **Estimate** running

## Purpose

**Single running log for everything discovered mid-implementation that must not derail the ticket in flight.**

While working any ticket, if you hit a bug, a missing piece, a wrong assumption, a pitfall, an
external constraint, or a scope gap — **do not fix it inline and do not silently drop it.** Append
it here as a comment and carry on with the ticket you are on.

Use `/backlog "<note>"` to append. Every entry must state where it was found so it is traceable.

## Entry format

```
### <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM> · found in <TICKET-ID> · <type>
**What:**        one line
**Impact:**      what breaks or is at risk
**Workaround:**  what we did instead (or "none — deferred")
**Action:**      fix now / fix Day 4 / accept as limitation / document in HLD
```

`<type>` ∈ `bug` · `gap` · `pitfall` · `constraint` · `assumption-wrong` · `perf` · `security` · `data-quality`

## Triage rule

- **Blocks the current ticket's AC** → fix now, and still log it here.
- **Breaks a later ticket** → log, and add a `blocker` note as a comment on that ticket.
- **Neither** → log and defer. Do not touch it.

## End-of-project use

Before submission this ticket is read in full and split into three lists:
1. **Fixed** — closed inline, referenced by commit
2. **Accepted limitations** → these go verbatim into the deck's *"What this system does not do"* slide
   and the HLD's *Assumptions & Constraints* section. This is where honesty scores points.
3. **Future roadmap** → these go into the deck's *Future Vision / Roadmap* dimension

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Every entry follows the format above and names its source ticket
- [ ] At submission time, all entries are triaged into one of the three lists
- [ ] Accepted limitations appear in the deck and HLD
- [ ] Roadmap items appear in the Future Roadmap dimension

## Deliverables

- `docs/limitations.md` — generated from this ticket's accepted-limitation entries
- `docs/roadmap.md` — generated from this ticket's roadmap entries

## Validation Gate

- [ ] `docs/limitations.md` and `docs/roadmap.md` exist and are non-empty
- [ ] Zero untriaged entries remain

## 🎉 Add`Smart Heading` Recognition Feature For Word Document

Starting from v1.5.5, LightRAG's built-in DOCX parser introduces the **Smart Heading** feature -- enabling better section-based chunking even for poorly formatted DOCX documents.

Many DOCX documents have visually clear section structures but lack properly configured Word outline levels, or retain incorrect heading styles from editing, copying, and concatenation processes. In the past, these issues could cause section titles to be treated as body text, or regular text to be misidentified as headings, resulting in chunking boundaries that deviate from the document's true semantic sections. For P chunking strategies that rely on heading structures, this creates fragmented context or mixed content from different sections, affecting subsequent indexing and retrieval.

**Smart Heading** targets such poorly formatted but semantically clear documents, restoring their true heading structures as much as possible:

1. **Recover Missing Section Titles**: Identify content that visually appears as titles but lacks properly configured outline levels, reducing loss of section structures.
2. **Reduce False Positives of Body Text as Headings**: Restore regular body text, complete clauses, captions, dates, and version notes that incorrectly carry heading styles back to body text, avoiding meaningless chunking boundaries.
3. **Improve Inconsistent Heading Hierarchies**: Reduce issues such as inconsistent sibling heading levels, inverted parent-child hierarchies, and skipped levels, making section structures more coherent.
4. **Distinguish Multiple Contents in Merged Documents**: Identify main titles and document boundaries of each piece of content, preventing section level interference between different documents.
5. **Reduce Noise from Long Tables of Contents**: Compress excessively long table of contents, minimizing the interference of duplicate information on indexing and retrieval.

By providing more reliable section structures for subsequent chunking, Smart Heading helps maintain semantic associations between titles and their corresponding body text, making chunking results align better with the document's original content organization.

## Summary

Add Hedera to the chain layer (`hedera`, `hedera-testnet`, EVM chain id 296 on testnet via the HashIO JSON-RPC relay), and stand up a **live x402-gated Mayarin service on Hedera testnet settled through the Blocky402 facilitator**, plus an agent that completes a real paid request against it end to end.

Target: the ETHOnline Hedera "AI & Agentic Payments" track (\$6,000, up to three teams at \$2,000).

## Motivation

The Hedera track is the only prize in this batch whose requirements are *literally* the x402 rail: host a live x402-gated service, have an agent discover and pay for it without an API key, settle through Blocky402. If the x402 core RFC lands, this is a chain addition and a facilitator adapter — not a product.

It also earns its keep architecturally. Blocky402 is the reason `X402Facilitator` has two implementations rather than one hard-coded local settler. A remote facilitator that Mayarin does not control is exactly the case that keeps the port honest, and it forces the "a facilitator is a signal, not truth" rule to be written down and tested rather than assumed.

## Goals

- `ChainId` covers `hedera` and `hedera-testnet`; `EVM_CHAIN_IDS` gains `295n` / `296n`; `caip2Of` yields `eip155:296`.
- `packages/providers/x402-blocky402` implements `X402Facilitator` against Blocky402's `/verify` and `/settle`.
- A real Mayarin endpoint is gated per call on Hedera testnet and is publicly reachable for the duration of judging.
- A demo agent pays it and receives the resource, with the settlement transaction visible on HashScan.
- Contracts, if any are deployed, verified on HashScan.

## Non-Goals

- Hedera's native `exact` scheme for HBAR and HTS tokens. Mayarin settles the **EVM USDC** path through Blocky402; adding a second scheme implementation in a 13-day window buys a second class of bugs and no extra prize.
- Hedera Consensus Service, Asset Tokenization Studio, and the Hedera Harness tracks. Different domain, not Mayarin.
- Mirror-node-specific indexing. If `eth_getLogs` through the relay is unusable, the answer is to not run `SettlementIndexer` on Hedera, not to write a Hedera-specific indexer.

## Specification

### Chain facts

- `CHAIN_IDS` gains `hedera`, `hedera-testnet`.
- `EVM_CHAIN_IDS`: mainnet `295n`, testnet `296n`.
- `MAINNET_CHAIN_IDS` gains `hedera`.
- viem chain definition via `defineChain` in `packages/providers/viem-chains/src/chains.ts`. Testnet RPC `https://testnet.hashio.io/api`, explorer HashScan.

`nativeCurrency` is HBAR with **18 decimals** over the EVM relay. Eight is the tinybar figure at the native Hedera layer; the JSON-RPC relay scales to weibars, and viem's own definition agrees. Corrected here after measuring — an earlier draft of this RFC said 8, which would have made every HBAR amount wrong by ten orders of magnitude.

### Blocky402 facilitator adapter

`packages/providers/x402-blocky402`, implementing the port from the x402 core RFC:

```ts
supports(network, scheme) -> network === "eip155:296" && scheme === "exact"
verify(payload, requirements) -> POST {facilitatorUrl}/verify
settle(payload, requirements) -> POST {facilitatorUrl}/settle
```

Request and response bodies are the spec v2 shapes verbatim (`{ x402Version, paymentPayload, paymentRequirements }` in; `VerifyResponse` / `SettleResponse` out). The adapter maps `invalidReason` and `errorReason` onto the `MayarinError` taxonomy; an unrecognised reason is a non-retryable `ExternalServiceError`, never a silent success.

**A `success: true` from Blocky402 does not settle a payment.** The clearing engine reads the returned `transaction` hash back from the chain before recording `ASSET_RECEIVED`, the same rule the codebase already applies to webhooks and adapter status. This is the one place the remote facilitator could otherwise mint value out of an HTTP response.

Configuration: `X402_FACILITATORS` as a per-network map (`Record<string, FacilitatorConfig>`), selected in `apps/api/src/container.ts`. Boot fails if a network
title: RFC: Hedera chain support and the Blocky402 facilitator — a live x402-gated service

## Summary

Index Mayarin's own settlement history as a subgraph, put the Subgraph MCP in
front of it, and let the paying agent **choose its rail from live data** instead
of guessing. Then replace `SettlementIndexer`'s `eth_getLogs` polling with the
same subgraph.

Target: two ETHOnline tracks, \$5,000 each — *Best AI Tooling or AI Use Case with
The Graph (Continuity)* and *Best Use of Composable or Standardized Graph
Products*.

Promoted from "cut for capacity" to a primary target. What changed is the agent:
the track explicitly wants AI agents, x402 payment tooling, and agents that
reason over live blockchain data, and #207 shipped all three.

## Motivation

A `402` from a Mayarin resource can offer the same price on two rails — USDC on
Arc and USDC on Base. **The payer has to pick one, and today it has nothing to
pick with.** First in the array wins, which is a coin toss dressed as a decision.

That is the gap The Graph fills, and it fills it load-bearingly rather than
decoratively: settlement latency and failure rate per chain are facts about the
recent past that only an index can answer cheaply. Remove the subgraph and the
agent is back to guessing.

There is a second, less glamorous reason that is the stronger argument for the
judges. `SettlementIndexer` polls `eth_getLogs` and advances 2.5 blocks per tick
against chains producing more than that — a known bottleneck: an hour of
downtime takes hours to work off, and a real outage never closes. A subgraph is
what that component wanted to be. Using The Graph as production infrastructure,
not as a demo lookup, is the honest answer to "is The Graph load-bearing here".

### Measured, not assumed

The Graph's own networks registry, read on 4 September, contradicts the summary
on its documentation page. What it actually says:

| Network | CAIP-2 | Subgraphs | Firehose | Substreams |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `base-sepolia` | `eip155:84532` | Studio | ✓ | ✓ |
| `arc-testnet` | `eip155:5042002` | Studio | — | — |
| `arc` | `eip155:5042` | Studio | — | — |
| Hedera | — | **absent entirely** | — | — |

Three consequences:

- **Nothing waits on #208.** `PaymentRouter` is already deployed on Base
  Sepolia, and Base Sepolia is a Studio network. The subgraph can index today.
- **Base Sepolia carries Substreams**, which is what makes the Composable track
  reachable — that track requires composing two or more Graph products.
- **Hedera is not indexable.** #209 gets nothing from this; the Graph story
  lives on Base Sepolia and Arc, and the submission should say so rather than
  imply coverage it does not have.

Incidentally, the registry's CAIP-2 ids are exactly what `caip2Of` already
emits, so network identity needs no translation layer. And it corroborates Arc
mainnet as `5042` from a second independent source — the id #215 deliberately
left out of `CHAIN_IDS` for being unverifiable against a live endpoint.

## Goals

- A subgraph over `PaymentCompleted` and `ResidueRefunded`, deployed to Subgraph
  Studio for `base-sepolia` and `arc-testnet`.
- Rail statistics an agent can act on: settlements, median latency and failure
  count per chain over a recent window.
- The Subgraph MCP in front of it, so the agent asks in natural language rather
  than hand-writing GraphQL.
- `RailSelector` — a seam in the payer client that turns those statistics into a
  chosen `PaymentRequirements` from the `accepts` array.
- `SettlementIndexer` able to read the subgraph instead of polling.
- The choice, and its reason, printed in the demo. An invisible decision
  convinces nobody.

## Non-Goals

- Hedera. It is not on the network registry and no amount of work changes that.
- Indexing anything but Mayarin's own contracts. A general-purpose payments
  subgraph is somebody else's project.
- Replacing the chain watcher. `WalletWatcher` reads pending transfers to
  addresses that may hold no history yet; a subgraph is the wrong shape for it.
  Only `SettlementIndexer` is in scope.
- Substreams beyond
title: RFC: Agent payment intelligence — index our own settlements, let the agent choose its rail

## Summary

Add Circle's **Arc** to the chain layer — `arc` and `arc-testnet` in `ChainId`, a local viem chain definition, and a `PaymentRouter` deployment on Arc testnet — then run the x402 rail on it with **Circle Agent Stack** agent wallets as the payer side.

Arc is the one chain in this batch where Mayarin's thesis and the chain's thesis are the same sentence: a USDC-native L1 where the gas token *is* USDC. Target for the ETHOnline Arc tracks (\$10,000 pool).

## Motivation

`CHAIN_IDS = ["base", "base-sepolia"]` (`packages/core/chain/src/types.ts:12`) is the only thing between the current deployment and any other EVM chain — everything downstream is already keyed by `ChainId`. The `feat/arbitrum-chain-support` branch proved the shape: 271 insertions, a `viem-chains` package, and four `Record<ChainId, Chain>` maps that the compiler forces you to grow. Arc rides that work rather than repeating it.

Why Arc specifically: Mayarin prices in fiat and settles in a stablecoin. On Arc the settlement asset and the gas asset are the same asset, which removes the one operational wart in the current deposit path — a treasury that must hold native ETH to broadcast, denominated in something the merchant never sees. It also removes the biggest objection to x402 micro-payments (see the gas question in the x402 RFC): the facilitator's gas is denominated in the thing it is already moving.

## Goals

- `ChainId` covers `arc` and `arc-testnet`; `EVM_CHAIN_IDS` and `caip2Of` cover them.
- A viem chain definition for Arc with `nativeCurrency.decimals = 6`.
- `PaymentRouter`, `TimelockController`, `DepositForwarderFactory` deployed and verified on Arc testnet.
- Both existing execution paths — contract and deposit-match — settle end to end on Arc testnet.
- The x402 `exact` scheme settles USDC on Arc through the local facilitator.
- A Circle Agent Stack agent wallet is the payer in the demo, spending under a Circle-defined policy.
- Ready to point at Arc mainnet on a config change alone.

## Non-Goals

- Cross-chain payment (payer on Arc, merchant settles on Base). Needs a bridge trust model; stays where `docs/roadmap.md` puts it.
- Circle Gateway nanopayments as a settlement path. Noted as the sub-cent escape hatch, specified separately if it earns its place.
- Arc mainnet deployment of record. What lands here is a throwaway v0, same rule as every other new-chain deployment.

## Specification

### Chain facts

- `CHAIN_IDS` gains `arc`, `arc-testnet`.
- `EVM_CHAIN_IDS` gains Arc testnet `5042002n` and the mainnet id, **both verified against the chain before merge** rather than taken from a blog post.
- `MAINNET_CHAIN_IDS` gains `arc` (the `isMainnetChain` helper from the Arbitrum branch, which must land first).

### viem chain definition

Arc has no `viem/chains` entry, so it needs a local `defineChain` in `packages/providers/viem-chains/src/chains.ts`:

```ts
export const arcTestnet = defineChain({
  id: 5042002,
  name: "Arc Testnet",
  nativeCurrency: { name: "USD Coin", symbol: "USDC", decimals: 18 },
  rpcUrls: { default: { http: ["https://rpc.testnet.arc.network"] } },
  blockExplorers: { default: { name: "Arcscan", url: "https://testnet.arcscan.app" } },
  testnet: true,
});
```

### One balance, two interfaces — the real hazard

Arc does not have a wrapped USDC. It has **one underlying balance exposed through two interfaces**:

| Interface | Decimals | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Native | **18** | gas accounting, native transfers, `msg.value` |
| ERC-20 precompile `0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000` | **6** | application transfers, approvals, allowances |

The conversion factor is `10^12`, the native balance is canonical, and the ERC-20 view truncates anything below `1e-6` USDC. Arc's own documentation states the rule directly: **do not model native USDC and ERC-20 USDC as separate holdings.**

For a double-entry ledger this is not a formatting note, it is a correctness requirement. Mayarin keys balances by `AssetCode`. I
title: RFC: Arc chain support and Circle Agent Stack — USDC-native settlement and agent wallets

**Counterpart to betmoar/cc-proxy-plugin#57 — the decision is ours, and this issue records the decision rather than deferring it.**

cc-proxy publishes `grade` on `GET /v1/models` and its comments name cc-operator as the consumer. We are not: `scripts/ops-tiers.sh:136-158` reads `data[].id` for an advisory membership note and nothing else (`grep -rn 'grade' scripts/ workflows/ commands/` — no hit). Their issue offers two honest resolutions; we pick one here.

## Decision: B — the field is not ours to read

**The user picks the model, cc-proxy routes it, operator decides neither.** That is the charter line, and this repo already paid to enforce it: 0.8.3 deleted the model-id catalogue from `check_routable` precisely because a curated table of another system's facts goes stale (measured against a live proxy: 8 route-fine ids refused — `docs/LANDMINES.md` _"A catalogue of another system's facts goes stale"_). Reading `grade` in `ops-tiers.sh` rebuilds, one layer up, the exact thing that deletion removed: `MODEL_GRADES` is a hand-curated table of another repo's judgments, and a wrong entry silently downgrades or over-trusts every dispatch that flows through `tiers.env`.

What `grade` would buy — "can an unfamiliar id carry judgment work" — is already answered at the right altitude: `tiers.env`'s seat→tier binding, which the USER writes, is where capability judgment belongs (charter: routing by task nature, judgment never below judgment tier). An advisory grade note would add a second, contradicting voice with no authority to resolve the conflict.

## What this means for the close

cc-proxy#57 route B asks the producer side to reword its comments and record "no programmatic consumer." This issue is the consumer-side record of that: **cc-operator deliberately does not read `grade`**, and if a future session wants to, it should reopen this decision rather than quietly add a reader — the reflex fix here is the same shape the 0.8.3 catalogue was.

No code change on our side. Not linking into any milestone; closing when cc-proxy#57 closes route-B.
title: Decision (counterpart to cc-proxy#57): we do not read grade — capability judgment stays in the user's tiers.env, not a curated table of another system's facts

## Overview

Replace AI-dependent code assistance with a **plugin-based language intelligence system** that uses official documentation, built-in linters, and static analysis. The bot provides code support without requiring paid APIs or external AI authentication. Users can host their own language plugins via GitHub repositories.

---

## Architecture

### Repository Structure

Both built-in (`helix-origin`) and community plugin repos use the same folder structure. The root `config.json` is the entry point the bot reads to discover all plugins in a repo.

```
plugins/
├── helix-origin/                    # Built-in plugins shipped with HELIX
│   ├── config.json                  # Repo-level manifest
│   ├── typescript/
│   │   ├── plugin.json              # Individual plugin manifest
│   │   ├── linter.ts
│   │   ├── patterns.ts
│   │   ├── docs-cache.ts
│   │   └── examples/
│   ├── python/
│   ├── javascript/
│   ├── csharp/
│   ├── gdscript/
│   ├── lua/
│   ├── rust/
│   ├── go/
│   ├── java/
│   ├── php/
│   ├── sql/
│   ├── html-css/
│   └── flutter-dart/
├── community/                       # User-installed from GitHub
│   └── <repo-name>/
│       ├── config.json              # Copied from cloned repo
│       └── <plugin-dirs>/
└── plugin-loader.ts
```

### Repository Config (`config.json`)

Root manifest for any plugin repository. Same schema for built-in and community repos.

```json
{
  "repository": "helix-origin",
  "name": "HELIX Official Language Plugins",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "Built-in language plugins for linting, documentation, and code analysis",
  "author": "HELIX-Origin",
  "plugins": [
    { "id": "typescript", "path": "./typescript" },
    { "id": "javascript", "path": "./javascript" },
    { "id": "python", "path": "./python" },
    { "id": "csharp", "path": "./csharp" },
    { "id": "gdscript", "path": "./gdscript" },
    { "id": "rust", "path": "./rust" },
    { "id": "go", "path": "./go" },
    { "id": "java", "path": "./java" },
    { "id": "php", "path": "./php" },
    { "id": "sql", "path": "./sql" },
    { "id": "html-css", "path": "./html-css" },
    { "id": "flutter-dart", "path": "./flutter-dart" },
    { "id": "lua", "path": "./lua" }
  ]
}
```

### Plugin Interface

Every language plugin implements a standard `LanguagePlugin` interface:
- `lint(code, fileName?)` — Static analysis with errors, warnings, doc links
- `explain(code)` — Line-by-line explanation using official documentation
- `suggestFixes(errors)` — Auto-fix suggestions for lint errors
- `getDocumentation(topic)` — Official doc cross-reference lookup
- `format?(code)` — Optional code formatting
- `getPatterns?()` — Common patterns and anti-patterns

### Plugin Manifest (`plugin.json`)
Each plugin folder has its own manifest:
```json
{
  "id": "typescript",
  "name": "TypeScript",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "TypeScript/JavaScript linting, documentation, and code analysis",
  "author": "HELIX",
  "fileExtensions": [".ts", ".tsx", ".js", ".jsx", ".mjs", ".cjs"],
  "docUrl": "https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/",
  "entry": "linter.ts",
  "capabilities": ["lint", "explain", "fixes", "docs", "format"],
  "dependencies": [],
  "repository": "https://github.com/HELIX-Origin/HELIX-CLI"
}
```

---

## Discord Commands

- `/lint` — Analyze code for errors (no AI needed)
- `/explain` — Explain code using documentation cross-reference (not AI)
- `/docs` — Look up official documentation for a language topic
- `/plugin` — Manage language plugins (list, install, remove, info)

---

### 1. Plugin System Core
- [ ] Repository config schema and validation (`src/plugins/repo-config.ts`)

- [ ] Plugin manifest schema validation (`src/plugins/manifest.ts`)
- [ ] Plugin loader with `import.meta.glob` discovery (`src/plugins/plugin-loader.ts`)
- [ ] Plugin registry with runtime enable/disable (`src/plugins/registry.ts`)

## Destination

Make Praxis a measurably excellent local-first, single-user CLI coding agent. Every core iteration must be evaluated against hermetic coding tasks and preserved trajectory artifacts before it is accepted.

## Current evidence

- Active-turn steering and queued follow-up are implemented in #523 and form part of the baseline.
- Praxis already has strong permission/sandbox, tool scheduling, append-only native transcripts, compaction, agents, hooks, MCP, and package/performance gates.
- The current plugin eval implementation already provides isolated runs, runtime event traces, graders, pass rates, cost accounting, timeouts, and artifacts, but it is plugin-oriented and does not score repository mutations or verification commands as coding outcomes.
- Open reliability and efficiency work includes #138, #121, #126, #147, and #152.

## Fixed product boundaries

- Remain local-first, single-user, native-data-plane, and CLI-only.
- Do not add accounts, organizations, RBAC, billing, remote control, IDE surfaces, or a telemetry control plane.
- Keep tests hermetic from host provider/model/config overrides.
- Keep authoritative transcripts append-only and provider-neutral.
- Provider-specific optimizations stay behind capability-aware adapters.

## Dependency map

1. Outcome evaluation foundation
   - Project coding-task discovery and schema
   - Isolated fixture workspace
   - Runtime trajectory, workspace-diff, verification, and aggregate artifacts
   - Hard pass/fail scoring without paid judges
2. Reliability recovery
   - #138 recover malformed tool input without losing the turn
   - #121 split connect/idle/total timeouts and define safe fallback behavior
3. Tool and context efficiency
   - Split ToolSearch/deferred activation from the broad #126 surface
   - #147 bound MCP descriptions and large text results
   - #152 make git context bounded, volatile, and worktree-aware
4. Provider-native depth
   - Public API-key Responses adapter
   - Turn-scoped provider client state and explicit transport fallback
   - Reasoning/tool continuation fixtures
5. Turn-kernel deepening
   - Extract TurnCoordinator, ContextPreparation, TurnPersistence, and TurnAccounting behind characterization tests
   - Add history rewrite generation and stable local embedding/protocol surface
6. Outcome-driven optimization
   - Evaluate ApplyPatch, LSP discovery, search, startup/distribution, and cross-platform work before admission

## Acceptance metrics

- Coding fixtures record pass/fail, verification results, changed/forbidden paths, turns, usage, cost availability, duration, approvals, tool errors, and retry/termination state.
- Every benchmark run writes versioned local artifacts sufficient to diagnose a regression without a remote service.
- Runtime changes cannot be claimed as improvements without a recorded baseline/candidate comparison.
- Required package, security, performance, and native gates remain green.

## Out of scope

- Product telemetry uploads or hosted dashboards
- Cross-user benchmark services
- Exact Claude Code UI/command parity
- A big-bang rewrite of `session-service.ts`
- Treating LLM-judge opinion as a substitute for repository tests and deterministic checks

## Execution policy

Implement one focused child issue and PR at a time. Keep shared contracts, generated outputs, and the main worktree sequential. Record merged child issues and measured decisions in this map.
title: roadmap: make Praxis outcome-driven as a coding agent

## The rule

The owner delegated **CPO** and **CTO** authority and stepped off the terminal. Decisions therefore
get made without them, and in conversation they scroll past and become invisible.

**Every decision made under delegated authority is appended to the table below — with who made it —
BEFORE work proceeds on it.** No exceptions for decisions that feel obvious. A decision that is not
on this page did not happen, and anyone is entitled to reverse it on that basis.

Append, never edit in place. If a decision is reversed, add a new row recording the reversal and
leave the original standing.

**This repository will become public.** Do not write the private sibling project's name, or any
personal email address, into this page — cite #47, which holds that evidence deliberately.

See also: **#148** (road to v1 — the steps these decisions shape) and **#150** (how status is
reported, and the commands that produce it).

---

## Decision log

| Decision | Rationale (one line) | Authority | Date | Reversible? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The product name is **Watchtower** | Owner's call, taken directly. | OWNER | 2026-08-03 | Yes today — nothing is published |
| **GitHub issues are the only tracker.** `checklist.json` is not | One record, on the repository, readable by anyone who lands here. | OWNER | 2026-08-03 | Yes |

I'll start by saying that I've tried many TTS models for voice cloning and dubbing.

I've encountered this common problem: when dubbing a sentence, the last word spoken is often cut off, or the speech stops before the sentence ends.

I'm sure TTS models are excellent, because I've also tried them to generate simple text-to-speech. So the model itself works well.

The problem is text-to-speech during dubbing. More stringent rules should be set, such as requiring it to finish all words correctly and not cut them off. Furthermore, for example, you could leave some leeway in the timing of sentences, so that it has a safety margin to finish words and sentences.

I don't know if this is feasible, but I'm noticing that it's a shame to have all these TTS models that clone excellently, and then end up with incorrect results. Even re-dubbing often fails to produce a correct and decently pronounced sentence.

I therefore believe that, with current TTS models, the level is already very high, and there's no point in adding new ones if we don't focus on and improve the final result.

I therefore ask that we move on to a careful review of the final result, improving the speech processing. Now, in my opinion, is the time to focus. I'm sure that improving this phase will improve the processing across all the various TTS models.

I would also recommend improving the speech speed: I've often noticed that the speaker speaks slowly, and as a result, there's not enough time to pronounce all the words in the sentence.
In fact, I would even consider setting a default speed-up rule to ensure that words aren't cut off (I don't know, it's just an idea).

Unfortunately, the result isn't usable today.
title: [bug] Improve the timing and quality of voice cloning

## Best-fit funding route

Primary: **Solana Foundation × Finternet Instagrants** (global, up to 10k USDG/USDC equivalent, open-source proof of work, typically fast review).

Secondary: **Solana x Cal Grants** (United States, up to 10k USDG) if the Finternet panel says the scope is too infrastructure-specific.

Do not submit both versions simultaneously without disclosing the overlap.

## One-line proposal

Build an open reference implementation and conformance suite for **cap → stream → settle actual usage** on Solana, using OCM inference as the real workload and covering cancellation, retries, provider failover, refunds and ambiguous settlement recovery.

## Why this is needed

Usage-based HTTP services cannot know their final charge before work is consumed. This is especially visible in LLM token billing, but the same primitive applies to bandwidth, storage, RPC and other metered services.

The network-neutral x402 `upto` scheme defines the core behavior, and active SVM work exists in x402 issue #1642 and `solana-foundation/pay-kit` issue #175. What is still valuable is an independent, reproducible workload that tests the complete failure surface rather than a happy-path payment demo.

## Existing proof of work

OCM PR #44 already provides:

- an OpenAI-compatible inference gateway;
- SSE streaming and cancellation;
- provider routing and pre-response failover;
- gateway-side metering and an append-only ledger;
- 33 tests;
- real Apple M4 / MLX validation through the unmodified OpenAI Python SDK.

The grant funds the Solana settlement and conformance layer, not the already-built gateway.

## Public-good deliverables

### M1 — Meter receipt and threat model

- Specify a deterministic usage receipt: request ID, authorization/cap, price schedule, metered units, actual amount, provider, timing, completion state and failover lineage.
- Define signed/hashed boundaries and what must never be trusted from a provider.
- Document cancellation, timeout, replay, stale-provider and facilitator-uncertainty failure states.

### M2 — SVM reference adapter

- Implement one open adapter against the most viable current SVM `upto` path, coordinated with Faremeter/x402/pay-kit maintainers where possible.
- Support authorize maximum → stream service → settle actual amount.
- Keep payment code isolated from the OCM gateway so other metered HTTP services can reuse it.
- Use testnet/devnet and capped amounts until the security properties are proven.

### M3 — Conformance and recovery suite

Automate at least these cases:

- normal completion below cap;
- completion exactly at cap;
- client cancellation before first token and midstream;
- provider failure before response and midstream;
- provider failover without double charging;
- repeated client request / idempotency collision;
- facilitator timeout with later on-chain confirmation;
- replayed authorization;
- settlement above cap;
- meter/ledger write failure;
- refund or zero-charge path;
- malformed or dishonest provider usage report.

Publish fixtures, expected outcomes and transaction references.

### M4 — Public demo and integration guide

- A reproducible OCM endpoint and client showing payment-required → authorization → SSE stream → final usage settlement.
- OpenAPI/example-client documentation.
- Benchmarks for payment latency and settlement overhead relative to inference time.
- A concise adoption guide for inference, RPC, storage or bandwidth services.

## Six-week milestone budget — 10,000

- 2,000 — receipt schema, threat model and failure taxonomy
- 3,000 — SVM adapter and facilitator integration
- 2,500 — conformance/recovery harness and transaction fixtures
- 1,500 — public reference deployment and observability
- 1,000 — documentation, demo and maintainer handoff

Reduce to 7,500 by removing the hosted reference deployment if the panel prefers a smaller first grant.

## Success criteria

- A permissively licensed public implementation.
- At least 40 automated protocol/integration
title: Grant packet: open SVM usage-based settlement fixture for OCM

### What would you like to be added?

This FR requests the implementation of a new SubAgent class: A re-usable component that manages LLM driven tool orchestration. 

This is applicable in the following contexts:
* Allowing a Tool to iteratively solve a problem it encounters. For example, the EditTool using the SubAgent to find a better match string in the case of stale data; or a future "update docstrings" tool, which may call multiple existing tools to find files, edit them and test them.
* Agentic Scopes - Allowing a Tool to be run in an isolated mode - If a tool doesn't manage its' own self healing, and instead expects to do that on the main thread, a SubAgent can be created, which clones the MonoAgent history, executes the tool, and only returns the successful response back to the main thread ()

This FR suggests the most direct path towards implementation would be:
* Create a wrapper around GeminiChat which can drive the GeminiChat::sendMessage*(..) functions either in a nonInteractive, or Interactive function
* Allow a list of filtered tools to be passed to the GeminiChat ContentGenerator::generateContentStream(..) function, so that only a subset of tools may be considered during execution
* Allow a custom system prompt to be provided for GeminiChat to use.
* Allow variable output via a set of private tools that the Agent can use to calculate response data to be accessed via the Caller of the SubAgent.





### Why is this needed?

Currently, GC uses a _mono-agent_ architecture; One SWE Agent which is responsible for all work across the application. While this approach is powerful in its' own right, there's some challenges that it presents:

* Higher Memory Rot - Given that all self healing operations occur in a single History object, there's a higher chance of hallucinations over time as the context history becomes more complex and full of conflicting / stale information. Consider the situation where a file-read occurs, then 2-3 edit attempts that fail, followed by a success. There now may be 5 examples of the same block of code in history memory, which can lead to confusion.
* Lack of SmartTools - The GC Codebase currently has a single agent implementation (GeminiClient + GeminiChat), which means that tools themselves cannot currently support agentic loops in their processing (e.g. recovering from a failure, or orchestrating private tools to execute a task). Further, no other part of the application can engage in Agentic patterns, since there's no primitive to leverage to do so.

### Additional context

Areas of open discussion:
* **Tool permissions** - There's some open discussion that needs to be had about how tool-based permissions work inside subagents. (For example, if you've given ToolX permission to write-always, does that permission also follow forward to when that tool is used inside of a subagent?) 
* **System prompt re-use** - The SubAgent can accept a custom system prompt to drive work, but it may be viable to leverage existing portions of the existing MonoAgent prompt. This is a challenge because the current Mono-Agent system prompt is _powerful_ but also _static_: It currently does not provide a mechanism to be re-used by sub agents, or be broken up in the case of available tools changing. In this case, an ideal solution for SubAgents orchestrating the existing tools may require breaking up prompts.ts to provide a sub-agent the ability to grab examples & multi-shot snippets for a specific tool it is using (which is currently hard-coded into the main prompt).

Important Notes:
* This FR _only_ discusses the addition of the SubAgent primitive, and is not intended to be a solution to larger discussions around mass orchestration of Agents, or their coordinated efforts towards task resolution (e.g. "why not use existing agent-orchestration library X?"). Those are significant architecture conversations that need to happen across the team, as orchestration is a higher level discussion to the SubAgent primitive

I swear to do honest, verifiable work on Frantic, respect claim windows, and stand by public receipts.

body_excerpt:
# 📝 Background

Several INT32 edge cases are not handled correctly in the integer division family on Wormhole and Blackhole. The primary known failure is INT32_MIN (-2147483648) flowing through the residual-correction path in truncating/flooring integer division. The same work should address the related INT_MIN correctness issues in tensor remainder and fmod, plus scalar dispatch and type-promotion behavior.

This can produce silent, finite, and plausible-looking numerical errors for otherwise valid int32 inputs. The existing investigation and reproducer are documented in [#51476](https://github.com/tenstorrent/tt-metal/issues/51476).

# 🎯 What Success Looks Like

- ttnn.div with int32 inputs and rounding_mode="trunc" or "floor" returns the reference result for INT32_MIN cases on both Wormhole and Blackhole, except for the documented undefined cases: division by zero and INT32_MIN / -1.
- The implementation handles both the residual magnitude and residual sign correctly; a value-only clamp is not sufficient.
- Tensor remainder and fmod handle the corresponding INT32_MIN edge cases with the agreed reference semantics.
- Integer tensors combined with integer scalars retain exact integer semantics.
- Integer tensors combined with floating-point scalars follow the intended FP32 promotion semantics.
- Wormhole and Blackhole agree on the supported input set.
- Regression tests cover tensor-tensor and tensor-scalar paths, both rounding modes, both architectures, positive and negative divisors, and divisors around the known failure thresholds.
- Existing behavior is unchanged for inputs outside the affected edge cases, and the fix does not introduce register spills or an unapproved performance regression.

# 💡 Problem to Solve

The int32 division kernels convert intermediate integer magnitudes to FP32 during quotient estimation and residual correction. INT32_MIN has the bit pattern 0x80000000; in the affected residual path, interpreting that magnitude through the existing conversion/sign logic can collapse the correction or apply it in the wrong direction.

The fix must preserve the existing fast path while making the INT_MIN value and sign handling correct on both Wormhole and Blackhole. The related remainder/fmod and scalar-dispatch paths must be audited rather than assuming that fixing div alone resolves the complete proposal.

Do not expand the bounty to the larger task of redesigning the LLK test harness to support negative operands unless the engineering team explicitly adds that work to scope.

# 🔎 Possible Approaches

- Reuse the existing INT_MIN-safe conversion pattern already present in the division kernels, while separately preserving the correct residual sign.
- Add explicit regression vectors for INT32_MIN with divisors around the Wormhole and Blackhole quotient-estimation thresholds, both signs, and both rounding modes.
- Audit the remainder/fmod kernels and scalar overloads for the same two's-complement and promotion assumptions.
- Measure or otherwise verify that the implementation avoids register spills and does not introduce an unapproved performance regression.
- Implementation details are not prescribed. The acceptance criteria above are the basis for bounty review.


## This bounty is subject to the [Tenstorrent Bounty Terms & Conditions](https://docs.tenstorrent.com/bounty_terms.html).

### Summary
Concurrent invocations of `release_milestone` can operate on stale state and clobber each other. Add a version/nonce guard so a caller must present the current version, and stale writes are rejected.

### Why this matters
On-chain state races cause lost updates and exploitable inconsistencies. A version guard makes conflicts explicit and safe.

### Requirements
- Add a monotonic version to the guarded milestone escrow state, exposed via a read view.
- `release_milestone` requires the caller's expected version and bumps it atomically on success.
- Reject a mismatch with a typed `VersionConflict` error.
- Emit an event on the successful bump.

### Technical guidance
- Read-modify-write the version within the same invocation; never split it.
- Return the current version in the conflict error.

### Edge cases — **each must have a test**
- [ ] matching version -> succeeds and bumps
- [ ] stale version -> VersionConflict
- [ ] two operations from the same base -> one fails
- [ ] read view exposes the current version
- [ ] event emitted on success

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] All requirements and every edge case above implemented and covered by tests
- [ ] New unit **and** integration tests; existing tests still pass and no regressions
- [ ] Structured, typed errors (no leaked internals; stable codes)
- [ ] `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, and `cargo test` all pass locally
- [ ] Code follows the repo's existing conventions; no duplication or dead code

body_excerpt:
### Feature request


Add two reward functions to `trl.rewards`, both built on existing primitives:

1. **`get_length_scaled_accuracy_reward(alpha=0.5, incorrect_reward=-1.0, reasoning_delimiters=None)`** : a reward-function factory that wraps `reasoning_accuracy_reward` and scales the reward of *correct* completions by their length **relative to the other correct completions of the same prompt** (a z-score within the GRPO group). Implements the length-aware shaping from **GRPO-LEAD** (https://huggingface.co/papers/2504.09696).

2. **`graduated_format_reward(completions, **kwargs)`** : a graduated variant of `think_format_reward` that gives partial credit (`1.0 / 0.5 / 0.25 / 0.0`) for partial `<think>...</think>` structure, providing a denser signal during cold-start training when strict-format matches are rare.


### Motivation


**Length-scaled accuracy : how it differs from the existing `get_cosine_scaled_reward`.**
TRL already has [`get_cosine_scaled_reward`](https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/main/rewards#get_cosine_scaled_reward) (#6066), which also rewards shorter correct completions. The two are complementary, not redundant:

| | `get_cosine_scaled_reward` (existing) | `get_length_scaled_accuracy_reward` (proposed) |
|---|---|---|
| Length reference | **absolute** token count vs a fixed `max_len` budget | **group-relative** z-score among the prompt's correct completions |
| Needs a length budget? | yes (`max_len`) | no — adapts to each prompt's own length distribution |
| Shaping curve | cosine interpolation between fixed bounds | `exp(-alpha * z)`; a group's correct rewards have geometric mean `1.0` |
| Paper | Demystifying Long CoT | GRPO-LEAD |

The group-relative formulation is useful when there is no good global length budget (mixed-difficulty data): on an easy prompt where every completion is short, and on a hard prompt where every completion is long, GRPO-LEAD still applies the same relative pressure toward the shorter correct answers, because it standardizes within the group. A fixed `max_len` schedule cannot do that.

**Graduated format reward.** `think_format_reward` is binary: a completion that emits only `<think>` (or both tags in the wrong order) scores exactly `0.0`, identical to a completion with no tags at all. Early in training that signal is very sparse. A graduated version gives the policy a gradient to climb toward the target structure. Nothing equivalent exists in `trl.rewards` today.

Both functions follow existing conventions: `get_length_scaled_accuracy_reward` mirrors the picklable callable-class factory pattern of `get_cosine_scaled_reward` / `get_soft_overlong_punishment` (so it works under the async GRPO rollout worker), and `graduated_format_reward` sits alongside `think_format_reward`.


### Your contribution

I have an implementation ready (functions, docs, a `paper_index.md` entry for GRPO-LEAD that cross-references the cosine reward, and unit tests including a picklability test) and will open a PR referencing this issue.
title: [Feature] Reasoning reward utilities: group-relative length-scaled accuracy (GRPO-LEAD) + graduated format reward

## Purpose

**Single running log for everything discovered mid-implementation that must not derail the ticket in flight.**

While working any ticket, if you hit a bug, a missing piece, a wrong assumption, a pitfall, an
external constraint, or a scope gap — **do not fix it inline and do not silently drop it.** Append
it here as a comment and carry on with the ticket you are on.

Use `/backlog "<note>"` to append. Every entry must state where it was found so it is traceable.

## Entry format

```
### <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM> · found in <TICKET-ID> · <type>
**What:**        one line
**Impact:**      what breaks or is at risk
**Workaround:**  what we did instead (or "none — deferred")
**Action:**      fix now / fix Day 4 / accept as limitation / document in HLD
```

`<type>` ∈ `bug` · `gap` · `pitfall` · `constraint` · `assumption-wrong` · `perf` · `security` · `data-quality`

## Triage rule

- **Blocks the current ticket's AC** → fix now, and still log it here.
- **Breaks a later ticket** → log, and add a `blocker` note as a comment on that ticket.
- **Neither** → log and defer. Do not touch it.

## End-of-project use

Before submission this ticket is read in full and split into three lists:
1. **Fixed** — closed inline, referenced by commit
2. **Accepted limitations** → these go verbatim into the deck's *"What this system does not do"* slide

3. **Future roadmap** → these go into the deck's *Future Vision / Roadmap* dimension

- [ ] Roadmap items appear in the Future Roadmap dimension

- `docs/roadmap.md` — generated from this ticket's roadmap entries

- AnalysisVersions/RecommendationVersions,
- EvidenceEvents/RealityChecks,
- Quellen, Kompetenz, höherrangiges Recht/Schutzgrenzen,
- öffentliche Routen, Navigation, Overview-Projektion und Detailakten.

Fehlende Fachlayer nicht technisch erfinden. Vorhandenen Fachbestand niemals verkürzen oder verstecken.

## P0-3 Übersicht: Wirkungspotenzial klar sichtbar
Portalweit auf Wahlprogramm-, Koalitions-/Mandats-, Regierungs-, Parlament-, EU- und Länderübersichten muss die WÖk-Einordnung vor Prozessmetadaten verständlich sichtbar sein. Soweit fachlich freigegeben mindestens:
- qualitativer Wirkungspotenzialbefund,
- stärkste positive Potenziale,
- wichtigste materielle Risiken/Zielkonflikte,
- Evidenz/Unsicherheit getrennt von Richtung,
- Richtungsprofil nur für redaktionell/fachlich geprüfte Pfade,
- Nichtkompensation/Schutzgrenzen,
- **alle** freigegebenen Key Findings - keine `slice(0,2)`-Verkürzung,
- keine Partei-/Regierungs-Gesamtnote oder künstliche Saldierung.

Detailseiten müssen die vollständige freigegebene Fachakte und Quellen enthalten, nicht nur Mandats-/Fakten-Teaser.

## Summary

The tracking issue for the Buildathon submission itself: what the terms actually require, what is scored, what the payout is conditional on, and the deliverables that are not code. Read the dates first — they are not the ones the event page shows.

## What the terms say

From the [Terms & Conditions PDF](https://openhouse.arbitrum.io/singapore_version_open_house_buildathon_terms___conditions.pdf), organized by Project Moonshot Limited (HackQuest) on behalf of The Arbitrum Foundation.

### Dates — the PDF governs, and it disagrees with the event page

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Event period | 14 Sep 2026 – 4 Oct 2026 |
| **Submission deadline** | **1 Oct 2026, 11:59 PM SGT** |
| Winners announced | 4 Oct 2026, 05:00 PM SGT |

The event page advertises a submission window ending 4 Oct. The terms say 1 Oct. Plan against 1 Oct; a late submission "will not be accepted" (§3.2).

SGT is UTC+8. WIB is UTC+7, so the deadline is **1 Oct, 10:59 PM WIB**.

### Existing work is allowed — with a condition, and a contradiction

§3.1 requires a submission be "either original work first created **or existing work that has been adjusted during the Buildathon** (this shall mean more than trivial development of the code base)". §7.1 lists as a disqualification ground "submitting work that is not original **or modified during the Buildathon period**".

The Code of Conduct then says the opposite: "All coding, design, and creative output must be produced exclusively during the official Buildathon timeframe… actual development or implementation must not begin until the Buildathon has started."

§7.1 is the operative disqualification rule and it matches §3.1, so the reading is that a pre-existing project qualifies on non-trivial in-window development. But §7.1 also lets the Organizers disqualify for "any other behavior deemed inappropriate… in their sole discretion", and their decisions are final and unappealable (§7.3).

**Action: get this confirmed in writing on the event Discord before 14 September, and keep the answer.** This is the single largest risk to the submission and it costs one message to remove.

The consequence for planning is concrete: **the headline features must land between 14 September and 1 October**, not before. Work done now is foundation for an existing project — real, but not what §3.1 counts.

### Deployment requirement

§3.1: deployed on **Arbitrum Sepolia, Arbitrum One, or a custom Orbit chain**. Robinhood Chain is an Orbit chain, so it qualifies on its own.

### Judging criteria

- Innovation
- Technical implementation
- Use of Arbitrum technology
- Potential impact
- Presentation quality
- **Novelty projects receive a bonus consideration**

Decisions are final and cannot be appealed (§6.1.3).

Note what is on that list and what is not: "use of Arbitrum technology" is scored directly, and presentation quality carries the same weight as technical implementation. A correct system presented badly scores as a worse project.

### Prize structure and the payout condition that matters

Reserved slots, applying to every three-prize track (§6.2):

- at minimum 1 of 3 reserved for a project building on **Robinhood Chain**
- at minimum 1 of 3 reserved for a project building on **Arbitrum**

Payout is staged, and every track **except "Best Promising Products"** carries these conditions:

1. 25% on winning and executing a grant agreement with the Foundation
2. 25% at a check-in one month after signing — **subject to building exclusively on an Arbitrum Chain**
3. 50% on a successful **mainnet launch on an Arbitrum Chain** plus a mutually agreed KPI

Prizes are paid in USDC on Arbitrum One (§6.3.1), may require AML/KYC before release (§6.3.2), and are forfeited if the grant agreement is not signed (§6.3.3). A team prize is the same amount, divided (§6.2.2).

**The exclusivity clause is a business decision, not an engineering one.** Mayarin's contracts are on Base Sepolia today and the architecture is deliberately chain-agnostic. T
title: Buildathon submission — terms, scoring, payout conditions and deliverables
